subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
I do not intend to take up much of the time of the House in considering the statement presented by the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham). There is one thing however, I would like to point out in the first instance. I was interested in what the hon. gentleman said with regard to increased earnings on the Grand Trunk Pacific line. There were added earnings in that section which were to be expected, and the like applies also to the Transcontinental. There is no mystery as to why we have a larger percentage of earnings in connection with these lines than we have in connection with other lines in the system. Those lines were built without business feeders and in territories already largely occupied by railways, or, if not so occupied, of such a character that they did not produce freight. They now enjoy the traffic coming from the old Canadian Northern branch lines, particularly the prairie system of the Canadian Northern, where the loadings are good and the traffic heavy. Of course these increases are taking place. I point out to my hon. friend in this connection
that it is merely a matter of accounting, but that as a matter of fairness to the government system itself the earnings on that traffic ought not to be prorated in the ordinary way; the originating carrier, i.e. the prairie lines of the old Northern ought to have credit for business originated on their line and a weightier prorate, as in the case of ordinary railway business between different companies.
We had a question in the House the other day which my hon. friend took exception to, and I said at the time that I had some sympathy for the stand he took. That question had to do with the matter of details of some railway operation-the exact point I forget. I propose to draw to your attention, Mr. Speaker, the present unsatisfactory position in which not only the House but the system find themselves, with a view of ascertaining whether or not there is some sensible way in which the activities of parliament can be so co-ordinated with the operation of the National line that on the one hand parliamentary rights can still exist and on the other the railway system be allowed to carry on irrespective of political interference.
Let me say at the outset that if we are to make a success of the National Railways-and every decent Canadian is interested in seeing that this is done-we cannot look upon them as a mere controversial issue. I take peculiar interest in this matter. It was back in 1916 that I was a party to the report under which largely these lines were acquired, and, although that was some years ago I have not been able to change the conclusions I then came to. In the first place, Mr. Speaker, it is perfectly clear there is nothing immoral in public ownership as such. There is no difficulty in connection with the ownership of property. On the other hand, it is also perfectly clear that in every country outside of Prussia that has tried the experiment, political interference to a greater or less degree has militated against the success of the experiment, has resulted in either higher freight rates or poorer service. The fault did not lie by reason of the fact that instead of there being perhaps a couple of thousand private shareholders in the country, the whole people of the country were shareholders; the fault lay in the improper interference on political grounds, on local grounds, with the proper running of the system. We have had different kinds of public undertakings run, and successfully run, when we got away from direct parliamentary control. We have commissions run-

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
ning, and running successfully, the Ontario Hydro Electric, for instance; I could mention others, but it is not necessary. If we can once get away from making, as a matter of party politics on the floor of this House, a football of a great national asset, and see that it is properly run, we are making a long step in advance.
There are two schools of thought in connection with this matter, but I think that both schools-everybody-will agree that the first thing necessary is that there shall be no dispute, no mystery, no concealment as to what the actual performance of the country's property is. Now, as we have it to-day, we have not yet been able to take that first initial step. Why, there is dispute to-day even as to the meaning of that report which was tabled by my hon. friend last week, and the dispute still continues. Surely it is perfectly clear we ought to have certainty, that there should be no doubt as to what the truth is, that every one should know where we are going. Just to show the state of bewilderment the public are in, and to prove that these errors are not confined to the less intelligent members of the community, but are to be found even with the most intelligent, I am going to refer to the public press. The Montreal Gazette of the 29th of May makes the declaration that the Canadian National Railways had made a net improvement of $5,917,561 as a result of the year's operation; and on the same date, with information collected from the same report, by gentlemen sitting in the same gallery, the Ottawa Citizen says that the Canadian National made an improved showing of $12,000,000 as compared with the previous year. We must try and find out what the truth is; we can never make progress without it. Doubt still remains. Why, in this morning's Montreal Gazette, Sir Henry Thornton, in a rather lengthy newspaper interview which he gave in effect, says that both these gentlemen do him grave injustice, because, he says, there was an increase in his net income, if I remember rightly, of $20,000, 000 or $21,000,000; at least $20,000,000. Obviously we ought to get such a report, such information, for the House that there ought to be no room for argument as to what the truth is.
Now then, let us go back to what the two different schools of thought are. I am going to an authority that my hon. friends on the government benches will immediately accept. I am going to take the considered utterances of my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) as showing what one school thinks in connection with this question of railway administration, an administration than 
which, according to them, must of necessity be a matter of controversy in the House, and a matter of party politics. I first read from Hansard of 1920, page 1669. The right hon. the present Prime Minister then said:
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to take up the time of the House, but I think it is important that the country should clearly understand the amazing doctrine that the government has put forward this evening as regards public ownership, especially as the government prides itself somewhat on having gone in for public ownership on a scale that no country has attempted or even thought of. Unless I am completely mistaken, the significance of all that has been said by the Minister of Railways, the Minister of Marine and the Minister of the Interior, has been to the effect that with the extension of government ownership, there is to be, not an increase of publicity, but a diminution of publicity in regard to matters pertaining to operation.
On the next page, the right hon. gentleman is reported as saying:
Again, I must say to the House that if any hon. member will take the trouble to look at Hansard tomorrow, I thir.k he will find that the expression the Minister of the Interior used was "enterprises of limited scope," and in that connection he referred particularly to the Intercolonial railway; he said that it was all right as regards enterprises of limited scope for a minister to come down and give to parliament a detailed account, but when we got beyond these "enterprises of limited scope," in other words, when we got into these vast undertakings in which this government has landed the country then we were to have something different; we were to have corporate management as private business enterprises were conducted.
Again he says:
The point to which I wish to direct the attention of the House is that it should be a matter of principle that there is nothing connected with the properties that the people of Canada own that the people's representatives in this parliament should not have a right to inquire into, not at one particular time, but at all times. That is a principle which the people of this country will expect to see respected in this parliament.
Now I stop just at that point. I do not adopt the principles laid down by the right hon. gentleman. I do want to see, if possible, some method by which the people's representatives, charged as they are with the safekeeping of the people's money, may satisfy themselves that substantially all is well, and at the same time maintain such a position as will enable this business-just as was said by my right hon. friend we were then trying to do-to be carried on as by a private corporation, without political interference. My hon. friend went on to say-and I wish to point this out because it has unmistakable significance; I want to dissociate myself from the proposition at once-that parliament should have a right to make inquiry not only at one particular time but at all times, that it was a matter of very great moment.
I point out to the House that if what was then sought to be done could be done, if to-day's current business was to be made pub-

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
lie, the National system, competitive as it is with the Canadian Pacific, could not be carried on-it simply could not be done. What we want to do, then, was to see that information was given the House, but at such a time that it could not place the system in a position of disadvantage in connection with its current business:	In other words current
operations and current business were to be regarded as a sealed book. My right hon. friend could not agree with us at that time and went entirely too far, I think, in the opposite direction. He goes on to say:
That is a principle which the people of this country will expect to see respected in this parliament. If government ownership is to mean that there is to be less and less in the way of publicity, a good many who have been advocating government ownership will think twice before they continue their advocacy. I ask the ministry what is there that can be done, if it is done in an honest and straightforward way, that will suffer from publicity? What is there to be feared from publicity ?
Well, I have no doubt those were the honest convictions of my right hon. friend at that time, but I am sure they are not his convictions to-day. Everything he says there is absolutely and entirely at variance with any idea of allowing the present directors free and unfettered management. I would also point this out: No matter how honest and straightforward Sir Henry Thornton may be it is possible that he would suffer from publicity, and it is possible he would have something to fear from it. Let me illustrate. When running a tremendous business in competition, as I have already said the railway president is interested in obtaining the very best quotations for supplies he can get, also in the strategic work that has to be undertaken-such a planning of lines, such a planning of private sidings, as will enable him to get as big a share as possible of competitive business. But every move on his part in connection with private sidings and the proper laying out of the system would be negatived if the publicity which the right hon. gentleman has urged should be adopted. My right hon. friend's question was answered by the late Mr. Richardson, formerly member for Springfield who said "nothing." My right hon. friend then becomes more positive, the interpolation encourages him. He goes on to say:
The more extensive a business becomes the greater is the need for publicity.
Again he says:
The vaster an organization the greater the need of publicity. I say that the ministry is heading in the wrong direction when they seek to stifle the giving of information. Their aim should be to encourage wider and wider publicity in regard to public affairs.
That was the considered stand taken by the right hon. gentleman in the year 1920. After thinking the matter over for a year he becomes a little more emphatic, if it is possible to be more emphatic, because on March 22, 1921, he moved the following substantive resolution:
Subject to the reservation that in exceptional cases there may be documents of a confidential character which, in the public interest, may properly be withheld from publication, the House declares that it is the undoubted right of parliament to demand and receive copies of all reports, accounts, correspondence and papers, in relation to the management of every department of the public service including the affairs of the Canadian National railways, whether operating directly under the control of the department or under corporate form.
Hon. gentlemen will see that the resolution could not be more wide or more positive. In a word it puts the current business of the government railways exactly in the same position as the business of any other department, because so far as any other department of the government is concerned the minister can refuse at all times to bring down confidential papers and there have been such refusals. So that the whole idea and effect of the considered resolution introduced by my right hon. friend in the year 1921 was to put the operation of the Canadian National railways in exactly the same position as the operations of any department of the government. In speaking to the motion my right hon. friend said:
But when it comes to the public, who are the owners of the system, and who are to meet the liabilities for any shortages occasioned by its management, we are told that the representatives of the people in parliament shall not have the right to obtain information respecting essential matters of management and detail.
The hand is not to be taken off the management; direct management is to be interfered with. He goes on to say-[DOT]
We recognize that Canada has not been faced, except during the period of the war, with a situation that was ever quite as grave as that which is produced by the railway problem to-day. It is certainly the first question pressing for solution, it is in every way the most baffling problem with which the country has been confronted. But the only way in which a problem of such magnitude can be solved, if it is to be solved at all, is through the people's representatives in parliament having the fullest information in regard to all its aspects.
I am afraid I will have to take direct issue with my right hon. friend there. I think that is going entirely too far. No useful purpose could be served by having every member given a whole lot of details in connection with railway management that he could not possibly understand-no one can unless he is a railroader. Furthermore if these details were given the railways could

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
not be earned on properly. My right hon. friend goes on to say:
Now, Sir, the reasonableness of the demand in this resolution, will, I think, be wholly apparent. All that the resolution requests, is, that as respects the Canadian National Railways, which are a branch of the government public service, this House shall have the same right as it has in respect to all other branches of the public service, vizthe right to the fullest information with respect to matters of great public concern. May I point out that the government's attitude in refusing to give this House any information, is really placing a premium, so far as the management of these railways are concerned, on inefficiency and on incapacity, if not also on absolute dishonesty.
Again I take sharp issue with my right hon. friend. He is going much further than the public interest requires; in fact if these ideas were to be applied we might as well give up all hope of doing anything with the National system. The present government are leaving matters very very largely as the late government did, but I wonder what the newspapers in the country would say if any member having a knowledge of the subject would get up and state that by reason of the fact that full details of the railway management cannot be obtained the government were really placing a premium on inefficiency so far as that management was concerned, and on incapacity, if not also on absolute dishonesty. My right hon. friend was wrong. I am referring now to Hansard for the year 1921, page 1179. He goes on to say:
I should also like to say that it is unfair to that large body of the public who are advocating a system of government ownership, that facts respecting the operation of these roads should be withheld from parliament. This is not the time to argue the merits or demerits of public or private ownership: but it is just to all persons, whether they are advocates of private ownership or advocates of public ownership, that the fullest amount of information should be placed before parliament, so that an intelligent publio opinion way be formed as to which of the two methods is likely to prove more in the public interest.
The only argument the government has urged against giving information is the specious one that for it to do so would lead to the affairs of the National Kail-ways being brought into party politics, that it would lead to a political control of these roads. Let me say, Mr. Speaker, that I think the direct opposite is the truth. The danger of the railway system of Canada being used for political ends lies in the fact that their operation is being surrounded by the secrecy with which the government is surrounding it at the present time. The one and only safeguard against political interference and control is the frankest, freest, and fullest publicity in regard to all the affairs of these railways.
Just let me paraphrase for a minute. In other words; the only way that the operations of the Department of Public Works shall be run by its political management, free from all its political control is that the frankest and freest and fullest publicity in regard to all the affairs under the Department of Public Works

should be given. I wonder if any one will get up and say, without the risk of cracking his lips, that there is any government that is free from political influence. And yet we have the full information in connection with these departments-at least we ought to have it; we do not always get it I admit, but I do not think the hon. member will quarrel with me if I say that at least he is going to change his view as there expressed. Now my right hon. friend was not alone in those opinions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
Is all that
my hon. friend has read not in the nature of a reply to an attitude on the part of the government of refusing any information?

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
Oh no, my right hon. friend is quite wrong. He is here speaking in advocacy of his own motion, to see to it that there is no privacy, that there is a right of public information, and that the smallest act of anybody in connection with the railways, even if done yesterday, should be made the subject of a debate in the House to-day, if thought desirable. He must remember that the issue is very very plain.
I am going a bit further. I think the wisest thing my right hon. friend can do is to adopt the stand taken by the previous government, to prevent the doing of just what he then wanted to do. He did not want it stopped; then he is in the position of responsibility and he wants to stop it now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
I cannot
admit what the hon. member is saying at all. I do not wish to stop it.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
The Minister of Railways certainly does want to stop it. He stopped answers, and I think properly so. But if it be the policy of the government to throw down all the fences, so far as the Canadian National is concerned, they certainly have not shown any evidence of that during the last two or three years. Oh, no. What has been done is, in effect, precisely what has been done before, but without any clear principles or understanding. In order that there may be no misunderstanding in regard to where I stand, the position of the late government was, that, so far as matters of management and operation were concerned, the fullest possible freedom was to be '	4. p.m. given to the directors; that the
House was not to have the right to get details from day to day of current matters of operation and management, current contract prices and the like; that they were not as of right to be in the position to say that some little thing is done wrong at this particular siding, or that the station at another

CJSl.R.-Minister's Statement
point should be better than it is, and that sort of thing; but that so far as matters of capital were concerned, new work, extensions in the field of operation, and the like, this House had to give its consent and approbation before the new work could be started or new capital expended. But we went further than that, Mr. Speaker. Our position was that the only thing we wanted to do was to leave things in such a way that the management was to carry on without interference with the current business; but that so soon as the current business was over and became a matter of the past, and there could be no possible injury done to the management, then parliament had a right to the information. That is one of the things my right hon. friend was referring to in his speech when he said that they were not entitled to information, at some particular time, but were entitled to it at all times. I really think he would be well advised to lay down clear and decisive lines on which information should or should not be given in connection with the railway. With a good deal of deference, Mr. Speaker, I venture to suggest that he will not be able to go further in the interests of the public than, his predecessors did; he is certainly not doing it to-day. He is certainly protecting Sir Henry Thornton and his directorate today.
But my hon. friend's views, as I have quoted them, are not peculiar to himself and his party. The right hon. Minister of Finance {Mr. Fielding) went, if anything, further- well I do not know that he could go further, but if he could he would have done so. I think it would be hard to find any member of my hon. friend's party who did not take exactly the same view. When the resolution was pressed to a vote he got the whole of his party to vote for it and if I am not mistaken he captured one or two Progressives in that particular vote. The whole strength of my hon. friend's party was represented either in that vote or in those commitments, and one interesting statement was made by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster), who at that time supported my right hon. friend with all his well known force and vehemence in this demand for publicity. He went a step further in the matter to which reference was made by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) in his speech the other day-information given to shareholders. The hon. member for Brome took the position that the people of Canada, who had to bear the loss or were to profit by the gain, were in a somewhat different position from ordinary shareholders inasmuch as, so to speak, they
were constrained to be such; and in view of that fact they had infinitely more right to information than had the ordinary shareholder. That is one view of this question. I think I am right in saying that whatever my right hon. friend may think as a matter of principle, he does not to-day adhere in practice to the views he then held. And, certainly, if he did adhere to them it would be much better for him, in the public interest, to refrain from giving effect to them but rather to support his colleague the Minister of Railways, who from time to time has objected to information being given out. Why, Sir, only to-day we have had two cases of this kind in connection with a matter far more open to inquiry than was any one of the questions to which we when in office offered objection. And what were these two cases? The first was as to whether Mr. Stewart was attending as a director, and how often he had been present; and the second one was a broader question which would include all the directors, information being sought regarding their diligence in attendance. A matter of this kind has absolutely nothing to do with the details of the company's business, and the answers to these questions could not help any one interested in the Canadian Pacific Railway or any one who might want to know, for purposes of competition, what the company was doing. Nevertheless the minister refuses the information. I think my hon. friend went a bit too far in this connection.
Mr .GRAHAM: I did not refuse. The president took exception to the question, and at all events he would not care to give information until he had consulted the board.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext: May I point out that this is the way in which the minister has refused all information? A return comes down conveying the intimation that the president or the directors think the information should not be given.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
My hon. friend had a right to adopt this general attitude. The former president took his stand openly, giving his reasons; and the late government absolutely supported him in that position, having regard, as I have said before, to all matters relating to current management and operation. Now, I think that the position the minister takes in regard to the two cases I have given is a mistaken one; and I also think it is a mistaken position which some others take, that simply because a man is made a director of the Canadian National Railways, or possibly president, therefore whatever he does is sacrosanct, and that any one who desires any information-yes, any

CJV.if.-Mmister's Statement
one who wants to do anything to better the system-commits a grave offence unless he acts upon their ipse dixit. Surely there is room for a common sense stand in connection with this matter; surely it must be right that the activities of these gentlemen should be open to investigation like those of any one else who some day has to be checked up and to give an account; surely it is right that parliament, representing the people who have to supply the money for operating the system, should be able some time to make an inquiry, without doing any injury to current business, for the purpose of securing information to show where the money has gone and to find out whether things are as they ought to be. Why, to use the language of my right hon. friend when in opposition, if we did not disclose things from day to day in regard to current business we were courting inefficiency and inviting dishonesty. Well, I do not know what he would have said, and vei-y justifiably have said, if we had promulgated the present doctrine ourselves; I cannot attempt to describe the language my right hon. friend would use to designate such an attitude, because my vocabulary is entirely inadequate for the purpose.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am very genuinely interested in this question, and I say that obviously political management will never do; sooner or later parliament has to assume some responsibility, and it does so every time it votes money. My own original view was that while parliament should be given the information to which it was entitled, at the same time the trustees, as they were then called,-I make no distinction between trustees and directors, the difference being merely a matter of names-should be surrounded with all the safeguards that relate to a judge, as to removal. This question, Mr. Speaker, is not solved at all; my right hon. friend has not solved it. I certainly do not desire to speak in 'reference to the right hon. gentleman in any way that might possibly be regarded as offensive; and indeed this should not be a matter of party politics; but, I ask: What has my right hon. friend done? lie has got rid of a railway board on which there were Liberals and Conservatives and he has replaced it with a solid board of Iris supporters. There is no dispute about that; I am dealing with the new directorate which my right hon. friend has appointed.
