speechtext: Was there any member of that board, to which my hon. friend has referred, who was not a supporter of the Union government?

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
Tell us who
he was.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext: Perhaps my right hon. friend will remember Mr. Hamilton who resigned from the board to take a position in the Martin government of Saskatchewan.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext: Mention some member who did not resign.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext: The ones you got rid of.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext: I do not think we shall experience much difficulty in disposing of this question. Take Mr. Barnhill, of New Brunswick. There was a gentleman of whom, I venture to suggest no man either in this House or outside, who knew him, could say anything derogatory. He was a gentleman who was a lifelong supporter of Sir Wilfrid Laurier; in fact, they were great personal friends. Mr. Barnhill enjoyed the confidence of Sir Wilfrid Laurier to such an extent that he acted as Sir Wilfrid's nominee, if I remember rightly, in connection with two international commissions or arbitrations, one being the inquiry as to the St. John river boundary. I do not think any one in the world can truthfully say anything against that gentleman. He was not appointed because he was a Tory; he was not. If my right hon. friend wishes to state the contrary, I will sit down at once.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
I hope my
hon. friend will not interpret my remarks as being directed against the hon. gentleman. He made the statement that members of the present board happen to be Liberals, and I asked him to please name some of the members of the board which my right hon. friend appointed who were not supporters of the Union government.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
I have already
done that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext: I do not think so.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
Supposing, for
example, we had appointed to the board my right hon. friend's colleague, the Right Hon. Mr. Fielding, would he look upon that gentleman as a supporter of the Union government?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext: Why did you not put him on the board?

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
In the fullest
sense my right hon. friend knows that not one of those gentlemen were any more supporters of the Union government than was his desk-mate.

CJV.R.-Minister's Statement

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
Might I just
add, since my hon. friend mentions the name of Mr. Hamilton, that he was a supporter of the Union government.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext: ' I do not know whether he was or not.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
He was, as
a matter of fact.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
I will go a
step further:	We did, at any rate appoint
gentlemen whom my right hon. friend does not desire to say anything against. I respect his truth and caution. They were dismissed without any cause being assigned. I have not yet heard any attack upon Mr. Barnhill, or upon Mr. Wood, or upon Mr. Hobson, or upon Mr. Riley. But, never mind what distinctions may be drawn as to whether any of these gentlemen was supporting the Union government or not, I desire to point this out to my right hon. friend, that not one of those directors was a machine politician, not one of them ever took part in the conduct of an election, not one of them was ever a member of this House. In a word, they were not partisans.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I may
correct my hon. friend-he is wrong with respect to Mr. Hamilton. That gentleman is a politician and took part in the Unionist campaign of 1921.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext: A lot of Liberals did that too. '

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
But he was a director
of the Canadian National Board.
Sir HENRY" DRAYTON: Before he could do that he had to resign from the directorate. But I am talking about party hacks, about politicians of the stripe of Mr. Dawson from British Columbia, Mr. Talbot, and men of that ilk; I am talking about gentlemen who, everybody knows, had absolutely no qualification whatever, except a political qualification, for appointment on that board. I regret being drawn into this discussion by my right hon. friend, but it is a thing which, once started, can be gone into with considerable detail, if the House wants details; but I think it is a mistake; I wonder if we cannot get away from party politics for a few minutes; I wonder if this system is not big enough for -us to try to look at it on its merits. I think it is. The only solution so far offered by the government has been to get rid of the old board, men who certainly were not machine politicians, and to substitute for them another board that certainly cannot be looked upon in quite the same light. I have paused to see if I could not carry my right hon. friend a little apart from politics in the hope of trying to get something done in a constructive way in connection with this railway system.
Now, I take it that every one of my hon. friends, looking at this matter fairly, will not think it a desirable policy for the sort of charges which my right hon. friend made throughout the whole session while he was in opposition to be continued and the National system made a football of politics. That is not to be desired. Nor, on the other hand, is it to be desired that the country shall be met with a plain refusal, apart from matters of principle and the like, to do this or to do that. My hon. friend must see that he is not solving the question by appointing a board in which he has peculiar confidence, because he is always going to be where he is at present. The Canadian National Railways are going to be very much longer lived than my hon. friend's premiership; they are going to continue. Does my hon. friend think that if this doctrine is to be followed, namely, the appointment of a new board by the incoming premier-and that is all-sufficient-there is any hope for the success of the system? When in the ordinary course of events my hon. friend goes out of office, does he think it would be a good thing for the incoming premier to do just what he did-throw out practically everybody who knows anything about railroading and take chances with a new board? Does he think it is possible to take that course and make the system a success? Why, it would kill any private company. Only a company with treasury backing could survive such treatment. Surely my hon. friend will agree with me that that is not a good thing? Surely he will agree with me that we ought to get at some basis which will make for stability and security in the administration of the National Railways?
As I was saying in connection with the original report, my view was that the trustees to be there appointed ought to have the security of office of judges. I still think they ought to have that security of tenure. And the trustees so appointed should be gentlemen possessing a peculiar knowledge of railway administration and eminently fitted for the work. I went further in that report, and with a view of cutting out political interference 1 recommended that the board should be a self-perpetuating board. To-day all that, has been ignored by the government.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
Was that plan adopted
by the late government?
C.N.R.-Minister's Statement

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
I pointed out
that I did not make very much distinction in wording between "trustee" on the one hand . and "director" on the other. After all, it is the man you have under the hat that counts. They were pretty good men on the old board.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I still think that something can be done, and I beg to move the following amendment, a copy of which I have supplied to my hon. friend:
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the followng inserted in lieu thereof:
"A select standing committee on National Railways and shipping is hereby appointed to consider the estimates for the Canadian National Railw'ay system and the mercantile marine, and all questions involving new capital commitments and the disposition of properties and assets,-
Suppose we stop there for a minute. Does anyone think that our present enormous capital commitments ought to be increased without a vote of parliament? Ought we not to know about them? That is one thing. The next is this:	The directors have the
property only to administer; they have not the property to sell. But it is not so long ago-it was during this session-that the Minister of Railways told the House-yes, a return was brought down-that the directors to-day could sell the property, could get rid of the property which they had in their hands. Does anjmne think that would be the right thing to do?

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
That is, just like any
other railway company.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
There are distinctions there again in connection with railway companies. I think the answer my hon. friend gave was rather broad. It is perfectly true that the directors may sell odds and ends, things that are no longer of use. But my hon. friend went further; he seemed to think they could sell shares in the system. There are a whole lot of companies included in the National; these sub-companies are looked after directly by these gentlemen. The whole stock of the National itself is in our hands, and they could get rid of the properties of these subsidiary companies. There should not be any dispute on either of these two items. Certainly they give effect to what the Minister of Railways himself said in this House, that that power of sale ought to be taken away. The resolution continues:
-and that as well to said committee be referred during each session the annual report of the said system and mercantile marine for such inquiry as may be exercised by and with such powers of inquiry as are possessed by, the select standing committee on Public Accounts with relation to the Auditor Generals' report. 
Now, that is in connection with wound-up business, the business of a past year. The country will be able to see that its representatives carry out their statutory duties; that is all it means. It does not mean that any matter of current business can be gone into, and it ought not to be gone into. None of these powers should be used for the purpose of hampering the system; rather they should be used to aid and counsel it. Had there been a check like this there would have been no Scribe hotel transaction,, and is there any well wisher of the National Railways who is not sorry he ever heard the name "Scribe hotel"? So this provision is merely for the purpose of protecting, for the purpose of helping. Then:
And further, that said committee be entrusted to make recommendations to this House as to what further, if any, details or improvement of method should appear in said annual reports.
Is that necessary? Is it a good thing to have something definite? As I said at the outset, a thing of supreme importance is that there shall be no mystery about the results of public business, there should be no room for argument as to what the real income of the system is. A repetition of the spectacle to which I have already referred, that of two intelligent gentlemen representing two important papers disagreeing, would be impossible. Can we not do something useful in that way? Would it not be a first-rate thing for Sir Henry Thornton himself if everything was put so clearly that there would be no necessity for explanation, no necessity for radio talks and the like, no necessity for that kind of argument, because everybody would know exactly what the result of his work was? Personally, Mr. Speaker, I think that under that amendment no harm could be done. But, so anxious am I that all possibility of harm be removed that I add the following proviso:
Provided, however, that the whole of such powers shall be so limited that no matter of operation the inquiry into which would in the opinion of the management be prejudicial to the system shall, if the reasons for such opinion are deemed sufficient by the committee, be made a subject of inquiry; and that rule 10 be amended accordingly.
Let us pause and see how effectively the system is protected under that provision. The government always have a majority of the members in committee. In fact, it is about the only place the government ever have a majority.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
The divisions do not show that.

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
I am not looking at my friends to the left, Mr. Speaker; I am referring to the government-hon. gentlemen to your right; I will put it that way, I do not want to mix them up with the gentlemen who ought to be to your right. The government name the committees and they always have a majority there, and I say it is the only place they ever have a majority. Now, the hand of the committee is immediately stopped under that proviso if the management come forward and say:	" Do not
look into that; it is going to hurt us for such and such a reason." If the majority of members of the committee who support, or ought to be supporting, their administration agree with that view, there is an end to it.
I am not saying for one minute, Mr. Speaker, that this amendment does everything I would like to do; it does not. I would like to see it carried so much further that we could ensure real co-operation between the parties in connection with this big enterprise. That is what I would like to see; that is what I looked forward to in connection with my report. I would like to see a complete change made in this respect;
I would like to see, as a result of a conference between all the parties, the selection of non-partisan directors who would have the confidence not only of people of one particular shade or religious stripe, but of the country as a whole. We thought we had them on the old board. Well, I still think it is the right idea. Perhaps we could try again. Certainly, the country's interest is such that no stone ought to be left unturned, on the one hand to secure the maximun of protection to the Canadian ratepayer, and on the other hand to preserve to the management that full and free power of control and operation so necessary to the success of the system. If we ever had1 anything which justifies a most honest effort on our part, Mr. Speaker, tc try and do something for the biggest question that confronts the country, we have it now. I would like my hon. friends to think over what the issue really is, and tell us frankly on what ground they do not adopt any of these principles I am now advancing, and tell us frankly what principles ought to be adopted so that we can try some time at any rate to get our feet on ground that will be solid and understood in connection with this great undertaking. It is idle to say that the matter is settled, it is not; and it never can be settled by simply substituting the political friends of any party for the outgoing
set of directors. I do not care what the party may be, it cannot be done that way.
There is another reason why this committee ought to be appointed. I now refer to the Scribe hotel. I have had the opportunity of going through the file in connection with that. It is a very meagre file, Mr. Speaker, for so large a subject. It is perfectly wonderful how much intricate business can be carried in the heads of some gentlemen-perfectly marvellous, for this business is very intricate. I am going to give just a short review of the Scribe hotel transaction, showing how from time to time matters come up that not only justify but absolutely require the appointment of the committee I am now moving.
The first is a letter from Sir Henry Thornton to Mr. Roy, who is the representative of the government in Paris, in which he says:
I am anxious to provide the Canadian National Railways with adequate office accommodation and a proper representation in Paris, apart from purely traffic matters. We are already well represented there from that point of view.
I would pause there, Mr. Speaker, to point out that one would have thought that the assets and the moneys of the Canadian National Railways ought not to be charged with anything except railway traffic matters. That was the justification which was urged by my hon. friend the minister when this subject came up on the 7th of June last year. However, the whole of this starts in a letter from the president which contains the paragraph I have just read'.
Next, passing over an unimportant cable just acknowledging the letter and saying that Mr. Roy is writing, for the first time, in Mr. Roy's letter, we hear about Mr. Aronovici. In the first instance, Mr. Roy recommends the premises occupied by the Grande Cafe with the Jockey Club, and the Hotel Scribe, as a splendid place for headquarters. Then he goes on, and it seems to be quite clear whom he got his information from:
Mr. Aronovi?! tells me that you have asked him to take charge of your office in Paris. I know that he is a man of large experience and unbounded activity.
That is Mr. Roy's letter of March 9, 1923. He tells us in that letter that the whole of that building was announced for sale, and so on. The next I can find is a cable from Sir Henry Thornton to Mr. Roy in which he says:
Thanks for your letter, with your views.
Will proceed in accordance Thornton.
That is March 25. Nothing happens, and then on April 9 we have another cable from Sir Henry Thornton to Mr. Phillips;-his agent in London, England, as I recollect it; I do
C.N.R.-Minister's Statement

not know his initials; the cable only gives the surname. Sir Henry Thornton asks him to repeat to Mr. Roy in confidential cipher the following. Then he goes on to set out about this property: Purchase price, 30,000,000 francs; government tax of 3,600,000 francs; additional amount of 3,600,000 francs; total 37,200,000 francs; and 3,500,000 francs to adapt offices. He goes on:
Please say first whether you endorse proposition in principle, second whether you consider purchase price reasonable as I have no personal knowledge of Parisian property values. It will be necessary to move fairly quickly, as there is an option on property expiring April 20th.
Hon. gentlemen will be interested to know who the fortunate owner of that option was. It was Aronovici, the only gentleman, apparently, whose advice was taken as to the whole of this large transaction.
Here is an appeal from Sir Henry Thornton from Montreal to Mr. Phillips in London, to be passed on to Mr. Roy in Paris, so that Sir Henry Thornton, who knows nothing whatever about Parisian values, and is apparently in the hands of Aronovici, may find out what he ought to do. Well, Mr. Roy is fairly canny. He loves that building all right; he wants to get a first-rate site for his offices, bue he does not venture an opinion upon Parisian real estate values. He is a very wise gentleman. He cables on April 12, 1923:
Re Scribe property. Would be ideal one for our work. Would recommend it strongly if it could be bought on reasonable conditions.
He gives no advice to Sir Henry Thornton as to Parisian real estate values. By his own cable, Sir Henry himself knows nothing whatever about that, and he is left with Mr. Aronovici, and Mr. Aronovici apparently thought it was important enough to get to Montreal about. This holder of the option gets over to Montreal, has his talk apparently with Sir Henry Thornton, and then goes back to Paris. The next thing we know is that there is a cable from Sir Henry Thornton to Mr. Aronovici who had got home again:
Bank sending money to Morgan's with instructions to pay to you on receipt of deed to you and mortgage to us satisfactory to Phillips, London, who will come to see you. Bank will also require a demand note from you for whole amount as evidence of their advance which note this company guarantees you against.
Now, I pause to point out that there is nothing whatever on the file to show the value of this property in the slightest degree, or to show that Sir Henry Thornton ever got any information apart from Mr. Aronovici. I am not saying that he did not get it, I do not know, but it is extraordinary how much business some people can carry in their heads all the time. One would have thought

that if the slightest effort had 'been made to ascertain the real value of that property- apart from Mr. Aronovici, the owner of the option, the man making the deal, the man who was getting the profits-we would see some evidence of it on the file. Some time ago when I asked the question whether it was true or not that this property had been offered to the Canadian Pacific for $1,400,000, and refused by that company, the government's answer was that they "had not paid any attention to the rumour." I venture to say the government should have made inquiry if they were alive to their duty, in connection with this matter which is surrounded by suspicious circumstances everywhere as I shall point out. At any rate the minister did send his representative across to try and save something out of the mess. Did he not send over his deputy minister to try and make some deal with Aronovici and get the property out of his name? I venture to say the government did make inquiries about the statement that this property had been offered to the Canadian Pacific for $1,400,000.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext: I never heard of it.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
All I can say is that it was in the Montreal newspapers. The statement was made more than once without contradiction, and we want to have the opportunity of bringing someone from that railway before the committee and find out what the truth is. Because we are paying a vast amount more than that $1,400,000. Further, Mr. Speaker, the press of Paris has not been quiet about this matter. It was not the real owner of the property that was interested in the price got out of that option if the press of Paris are correct. If they are right there were some fifty-one shares, and I do not know how the option was fixed having regard to the number of shares. It may have been one hundred parts, it may have been more-I would have expected there would have been one hundred parts-but those fifty-one shares never got back to the persons that really owned the property. Well, here we have it. No advice to Sir Henry Thornton as to what that property is worth. The next thing we have on file is a cable from Sir Henry to Mr. Phillips:
Go to Paris immediately and see my letter of April 30 in hands of Arnold Aronovici of 2 Edouard VII street and get lawyer to approve title and deed to Aronovici and mortgage to this company. Matter to be closed Saturday.
There is another thing in connection with this matter that the House ought to inquire into. It is a serious thing to mislead the House. It is a serious thing to knowingly

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
make a misstatement to the House. Nevertheless the House was deceived last June. Misstatements were then made in parliament, and I want at the very inception to say that these misstatements were not the fault of the Minister of Railways. He was giving the facts as he was instructed. So far as I can see he was not responsible for the misstatement of the amount of the deposit; he was not responsible for the misstatement as to the syndicate. These are two material misstatements that he was not in any way responsible for. On the other hand he was fairly giving the House, according to his instructions, the fullest information that he had to give.
The next matter on the file that I wish to refer to is the letter of Sir Henry Thornton to Mr. Carson, the manager of the Bank of Toronto at Montreal. It is dated May 25, 1923, and reads as follows:
In connection with the advance made by your bank of 38,232,161 French francs-
Hon. gentlemen will remember this figure- -($2,608,330) to Arnold Aronovici, for which his note has been issued payable on demand at 6 per cent, funds have been deposited by the Canadian National Railways in a special account in the Montreal branch of the Bank of Toronto in the sum of $2,608,330.
We have the word of a minister on the 7th of last June, and on another occasion, that every cent of the deposit was this two millions. We were not told the truth, we were not told the facts, but the minister simply gave them to us as he understood them.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext: If I remember correctly I was asked the purchase price and gave the amount as approximately two millions. I had not the information concerning the additional amounts which went for taxes, transfers and the buying out of the rights of the tenants in this building. It must be remembered that in Europe a system of long term leases is in vogue, and when a property is purchased the leaseholders are asked to give their leaseholds, and they have to be paid large amounts as a consequence. This represents the extra amount over the $2,000,000. It was a little under two millions if I remember correctly, and did not include these last items which I have mentioned.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
The minister is wrong. AVhat I am referring to is the information he gave as to how this deal was financed. The fact is, we were told there was a deposit of $2,000,000. That is how it was done. It was an awful job getting it and we were all evening at it, but there was $2,000,000 deposited in that bank-that was the information the House got, and there is the letter. There is no use talking about tenants' rights and all 171
the rest of it, there was the deposit and the minister's statement, and there is the fact. This is how this deal is financed. This money is not to be withdrawn from the Bank of Toronto till the note and interest thereon is paid. This says:
You are authorized at any time to call for the payment of the said advance with interest after giving the General Treasurer of the Canadian National Railways five days' notice of your purpose so to do, and if the principal of the said note is defaulted you are empowered to apply the deposit to the liquidation of the defaulted principal.
Hon. gentlemen will note that; that money could be taken for the purpose of that note.
Any failure to pay the interest on the note is to be brought to our attention, but no part of the deposit is to be used for the discharge of this indebtedness.
There was just enough for the principal, but not enough for the interest. I pass on to the firkt information, as far as I can find, that the hon. minister ever got. I think his first information is contained in a letter dated May 31. Really, after all, what I am doing is showing very largely that he is not well treated in this letter in connection with this matter. I think that was his first information. I do not believe he was a party to this thing at all. I do not propose to read the whole letter. This letter is addressed from Sir Henry Thornton to the hon. minister, and reads in part:
Early in this month an opportunity developed to secure a property at the corner of Rue Scribe and Boulevard des Capucines, close to the Place de l'Opera, and in the centre of the banking and transportation district; briefly, it may be said that this location is in the very heart of the city.
I want to point out what a mistake it is to do business in that irregular way, without proper files, or if you have a file never to refer to it. Here on the 31st of May Sir Henry Thornton says:
An opportunity developed to secure a property- early in this month.
His own file shows he had it on the 9th of April. Why was the minister not taken into his confidence? Why was nothing said about it? Was Mr. Aronovici still here then? What was the trouble? But there is the excuse to the minister. He says:
Early in this month an opportunity developed to secure a property-
And I turn to the 9th April, and I find Sir Henry Thornton's own wire to Mr. Phillips of that date mentions the property and gives the price and asks Roy as to that. Well, there is just a month's delay. He says immediate action was necessary. Well it was not, with that month running on.
Immediate action was necessary as I had information from authentic sources that other interests were considering the property.



C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
We would like to learn what the date of the Canadian Pacific refusal was.
Accordingly I immediately arranged that an agent should purchase the property, and employed the support of the Canadian National Railway system in arranging suitable temporary financial credit.
He says:	"Suitable temporary financial
credit". You might well underline all those words.
The deal was immediately consummated.
Well, it was not. It was not consummated immediately after the 9th April, when it came up. The money was only paid up on the 25th May, as shown by his own letter. Nevertheless he says to the minister that the deal was immediately consummated.
And simultaneously negotiations were entered into with a responsible syndicate,-
There is where my hon. friend got this present information, or misinformation, in regard to the syndicate.
-not connected with the Canadian National Railway system, for the purpose of taking over the property and with a view to our becoming tenants. These arrangements have now been completed-
And there never was a syndicate or anybody outside of Mr. Aronovici, so far as the file shows, and I think my hon. friend knows that there was nobody but Aronovici, and no syndicate.
-and the syndicate has agreed to take over the property subject to certain details.
This is not the whole of the letter but simply portions. The letter continues:
I regard it as fortunate that the Canadian National Railway system has been able to secure such advantageous quarters at a reasonable rental without capital expenditure.
I do not know that I should go through the tortuous twistings of everything that they have tried to do in connection with this matter. The minister found such a mess that he had to send his deputy over. There is no dispute about these facts. I am reading from this very' incomplete file. Something is said every here and there which lets the thing out. Take for example the order in council, which says:
A property on the corner of the Rue Scribe and Boulevard des Capucines was proposed to the Canadian National Railway Company by Mr. Arnold Aronovici of Paris, who held an option over such property.
Is there any dispute as to who was making the money, and as to who had got the option, when the government's own order in council shows it was Mr. Aronovici?

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext: That is subsequent, is it?

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
Yes my hon.
friend is quite right. This is a summation of what Mr Graham Bell, the deputy, was able to find out and do. This appears in his report.

He had to be sent over twice, if not three times. It is hard to gather everything from this skimpy file, but my hon. friend knows the facts very well. Why, he made a settlement with Mr. Aronovici. He made a settlement with Mr. Aronovici in October, 1923- it does not seem to be complete yet. It has to be borne in mind that the Canadian National thought so much of Mr. Aronovici that, so far as the files show, not only did they buy from him the property he held under option without knowing anything about it, and without any advice as to what it was worth, but they left it in his name subject to a mortgage; and then of course found out apparently that he was not a man of the kind they could safely leave their property with, and they took it from him. They had to pay a great big sum of money in taxes when they took it from him, as the return shows. But a settlement was made with him about the time they took the property over, and this is about as much as I could get out of it. By the settlement of October, 1922, Mr. Aronovici receives, in order to liberate himself from all contracts he may have made up to the present time with any parties whatsoever with regard to the Palais Canadien, the sum of 650,000 francs.
For architectural work, plans, estimates and expenses-to be justified-in view of transforming the basements, ground floor, and first floor of the "Palais Canadien,'' 169,000 francs.
Article 3-The sum of 700,000 francs will be held at the disposal of Mr. Aronovici at the bank.
This makes a total of 36,751,161.75 francs To this must be added the claims of the Societe du Jockey Club, and of the Societe Francaise la Rente Fonciere.
And then we have all sorts of companies which I shall not weary the House by referring to. It seems to me that my hon. friend in the long run will simply have to submit a vote for the purpose of clearing up the whole mess. I do not believe he will be able to finance the thing; if he undertakes to do so he will only do it at a ruinous rate, and I should not be at all surprised to find something in the estimates to cover these expenditures.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext: There is nothing hidden or tucked away in the estimates; there is a conspicuous item covering the matter.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext: How much?

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
Three millions, if I remember correctly. The item, I say, is in the estimates, and that is the only proper way of dealing with the situation.

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
That is quite
right; and it is the conclusion I have come to myself. Attempts are made to bring in this and the other company; we are to have a French company, the Canadian Realty Company, the British Prudential Assurance Company, and the government guarantees all these concerns. My hon. friend is right in scrapping the whole mess; and none of these undertakings should be made the subject of order in council.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext: The order in council should have been rescinded, and I may observe that as a matter of fact we are not carrying on any operations by that method.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
I was about to point out that this should have been done before the estimates were submitted. But if the minister could abrogate the purchase it would be a good thing for the Canadian people. Is there no way by which that can be done? Have any inquiries been made regarding the solvency of Mr. Aronovici, and what possibility of success there would be in the event of action being brought against him? In short, has anything been done with a view to endeavouring to get our money back? That is the thing the purchase that ought to be rescinded. Now, Mr. Speaker, it is not necessary that I should go further in pointing out the absolute urgency of a committee to investigate this matter. This is an example of the things that must occur from time to time. I hope we shall never experience anything as bad again, but we must be on guard against its recurrence; and there should be some committee such as I propose to deal with matters of this kind. How much better it would have been for my hon. friend if there had been such a committee to which the House could have had recourse; for we could have obviated the inconvenience and annoyance that were caused last session when hon. members tried to get information which was not available. How much better it would have been had there been no necessity to crowd the order paper with questions, ever since parliament convened, in an endeavour to obtain the full facts regarding the Scribe hotel, which information we have not yet completely received, and to which parliament is entitled. How much better, I say, it would have been if there had been a committee to which the whole matter could have been referred. I think my hon. friend admitted in his speech that he would offer no objection to the question of the Scribe hotel being submitted to 1714
a committee. I may have misunderstood him, although I think he made that statement. But if he did not, at any rate I do not think he will now oppose the motion I am making. Without detaining the House further, Mr. Speaker, I move the motion which I have already read:
That a select standing committee on National Railways and Shipping is hereby appointed, to consider the estimates for the Canadian National Railway system and the Mercantile Marine, and all questions involving new capital commitments and the disposition of properties and assets, and that as well to said committee be referred during each session the annual reports of the said system and Mercantile Marine for such inquiry as may be exercised by, and with such powers of inquiry as are possessed by, the select standing committee on Public Accounts with relation to the Auditor General's report; and further, that said committee be entrusted to make recommendations to this House as to what further, if any, details or improvement of method should appear in said annual reports; provided, however, the whole of such powers shall be so limited that no matter of operation the inquiry into which would in the opinion of the management be prejudicial to the system shall, if the reasons for such opinion are deemed sufficient by the committee, be made a subject of inquiry; and that rule No. 10 be amended accordingly.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
Every one was interested in the report submitted by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) the other day. We have now a vast system of railways, the property of the Canadian people, which is capable of rendering great and important service to the country. Transportation and the Canadian National Railways together constitute what one may call one of the major problems that are now before the people of Canada. Every one recognizes the tremendous importance of transportation in this country, a country covering half a continent, a country of vast distances, a country of great agricultural and other communities situated perhaps almost in the centre of the continent. These facts indicate quite clearly the transcending importance of transportation to the prosperity of the Canadian people. We have a small population and without doubt our burden in connection with the National Railways is a heavy one to-day. We have 22,000 miles of steam-operated railways stretching from sea to sea, and there are naturally many things in connection with that great extent of railway that appeal to the popular imagination. The Canadian National Railway system is a vast experiment; it is something new in the history of the nations that a country with a population of less than 9,000,000 should have come into possession of a system of railways so widespread as the Canadian National Railways. I say, these railways are an experiment; but they are an experiment which the people of Canada are determined shall not fail. What

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
is the alternative? What faces us to-day? Shall that experiment prove a failure? I can hardly imagine what the situation would be if our Canadian National Railways should turn out to be a decided failure.	Those who
oppose public ownership of the railways surely have in mind some scheme which they could bring forward in the event of the Canadian National Railways not being successful. But for my part I cannot conceive of any private plan whereby this great national corporation could be successfully operated. What were the circumstances in which we found ourselves with respect to these railways? We did not wish public ownership upon ourselves; national ownership came as the result of the failure of private control. Now we cannot allow failure in the management of this system, and I am one of those who believe that the day is not far distant when we shall find the Canadian National Railways no longer a liability but a valuable asset.
With regard to the report submitted by the Minister of Railways, there seems to be some difference of opinion as to just what is the exact financial situation for the past year. I have prepared a summary of the statement, which I did not intend to place upon Hansard, but it seems to me to show quite clearly the financial result of the past year's operation. We were told that the gross revenue was $263,554,436, and the operating expenses were given at $242,366,973. This left a net revenue of $21,187,463. These figures represent all the lines operated by the Canadian National board. Against this net revenue we have charges for rent, taxes, and so forth, amounting to $7,822,585, leaving a net revenue of $13,364,875. The fixed charges were $66,144,226. If we subtract the net operating profits of $13,364,875, we have still a deficit of $52,779,351. Now, the deficit for 1922 was $58,691,911. So the betterment this year is $5,922,560, or in round figures, $6,000,000. That is the position, as far as I understand it, disclosed by the statement made by the Minister of Railways in his annual report of the system. We are not over the hill; a considerable difficulty still remains in front of us. A deficit of $52,000,000 is a large amount of money, but there is this encouragement that we are moving in the right direction, that each year the net operating profit is becoming larger, and we hope that in the not far distant future improvements will come so rapidly that we shall have a balanced budget meeting all the fixed charges.
I want to say a word or two here in connection with the Canadian Pacific Railway. There seems to be an impression in the minds of some people that there must necessarily be a spirit of anr^r. Forke.]
tagonism towards the Canadian Pacific when we look so anxiously for the success of the Canadian National Railways. Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to register a protest, as far as I am concerned, of harbouring any feeling of hostility towards the Canadian Pacific Railway. That railway is a great national institution, owned and operated by a private corporation, it is true; nevertheless it is, I repeat, a great national institution. And I want to be fair: Although Canada has done a good deal for the Canadian Pacific in the way of large land and other grants, still the Canadian Pacific has done something for Canada in return, and all of us I believe are proud of its achievements. Therefore I state emphatically that whatever I have to say in favour of the Canadian National Railways is prompted by no spirit of hostility towards the Canadian Pacific Railway. It would be a national calamity were the Canadian Pacific Railway to become a failure, just as it would be a national calamity should the Canadian National Railways not become prosperous in the not very far distant future. There is room in this vast country for these two magnificent railway systems. To me it is an ideal situation that we should have the public owning one great railway and a private corporation owning the other. There ought to be a healthy rivalry between these two great organizations, a rivalry which will be to their benefit and to the benefit of the country.
I think everyone will recognize the fact that during the last year or two there has been a vast improvement in the operation of the Canadian National Railways. Everyone will admit that to-day the service is much improved in every way. I do not think I can pay a better compliment to the publicly-owned railway than to say that I think the service is fully equal to that on the Canadian Pacific Railway; indeed I think that is a compliment to both railways. Service, it seems to me, has been the motto of the president of the Canadian National Railways and of his officers and employees. I am confident that everyone who has travelled on the Canadian National system during the last year or two will agree with me that the service is of the best. Even in the carriage of freight, good service has been rendered. I am not going to discuss freight rates at the present time; that is a question which can be discussed from a different angle. Last year the prairies raised the largest crop in their history, and I think that never before was such a crop handled more efficiently or with less friction-. So far as I

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
know there have been no serious complaints of shortage of cars and lack of transportation facilities with regard to the movement of that immense crop.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext: Will the speaker say that the service of 1921 was not the same as that of last year?-1921 was the first crop year the system had adequate facilities for handling the crop.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext: I am not inclined to make any very definite statement in that regard. The crop in 1921 was not as large anyway, and consequently the demand upon transportation facilities was not as severe as during last year.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext: The service was good.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext: It might have been-I am not finding any fault with the past management. But still I think any one without prejudice will admit that the service on the Canadian National Railways has improved tremendously during the last two years. Dealing with passenger traffic, I am sure there is no comparison to-day with what it was in 1921.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext: Passenger traffic?

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext: Yes. There is no comparison between the service rendered to-day on the Canadian National Railways and that of two years ago. It is not so many years ago that I had to wake up the conductor to let me off at a flag station. No such thing happens to-day?

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext: How long ago?

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext: Perhaps two or three years ago. I can assure my hon. friend that in going from Brandon to Scarth I had to shake the man by the shoulder and tell him to stop the train in order to let me get off. I do not think you could get worse service than that on any railway.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
That was not in 1923,
though.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
No, it was further back than that. It might have been the old Canadian Northern, but the facts are exactly as I have stated them. It was in the early morning, before daylight. All hands seemed to be asleep, and there was no chance, of getting off at the flag station unless you wakened some one up. That sort of thing does not occur to-day. Iam not making any complaint against the old board of management, but I think every one will recognize that the service is improved. The carriages are
clean; the trains are running pretty well on time; the dining and sleeping car services are good. In fact, I do not know that any complaint can be offered in regard to the service now being rendered.
It seemc-d to me that the annual report was a frank statement of affairs and that it gave us a very good idea of what the financial condition, of the railway is. I am not speaking from the point of view of a comparison of the present board with the previous board. The present board has been in office only a little over a year and a half and I would not claim that all the improvements that have taken place can be credited to them. Perhaps the board that went out did their part; perhaps they were doing the best they could to make the operations successful. But so far as I can see the people have reason to be proud of the present management and of the way the system is being operated. So far as the property is concerned, the ordinary layman is not in a position to criticise or to say whether or not it has been kept up to the highest mark-that is, in the way of engines, cars and all the equipment necessary to carry on a railway. But when we find good service, when we find the trains running on time, when we find all the requirements of the public being met, it is pretty good evidence that the property is being kept up in a fairly efficient manner. So far as the maintenance of the road is concerned, one can get a pretty good idea of what the road-bed is like by travelling over the railway from the prairie provinces to Ottawa. I am perfectly certain that that roadbed is in pretty good shape, judging from the smoothness with which the cars run over the rails. It is true, however, that a layman in criticising these matters is pretty much at sea and cannot speak with any definiteness.
As I have already said, we have a vast system of railways, comprising 22,000 miles and employing 100,000 persons; we have a telegraph system comprising 100,000 miles of wires; we have an express company reaching all over Canada; we have 60 vessels carrying the Canadian flag. Does any hon. member believe it is humanly possible that that vast system can be operated without some mistakes being made? It is perfectly evident that there will be mistakes, and those mistakes can be magnified and used in such a way as to be detrimental to the prosperity and the advancement of the railway. I do not think there should be any carping criticism in connection with the management. It is quite possible that if you begin to particularize or investigate very closely, in connection with a

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
system covering such a vast extent of territory, you can make a very good case in favour of a claim of mismanagement. But we have to judge the thing by and large; we have to judge by the results in the main, and I am sure we have good reason to be satisfied that things are being carried on very well. We can come to that conclusion when we see the improvement from the financial side and when we see the service that is being rendered in the matter of both freight and passenger traffic.
I noticed an article in the Montreal Star the other day with the heading "Two Speeches Against Government Ownership," referring to speeches made by the Minister of Railways and by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen). Well, you can draw almost any inference you like when you make up your mind to take a certain meaning from what an hon. member may say in the House. I am not prepared to agree with the Montreal Star that either the Minister of Railways or the leader of the opposition made a speech that was against national ownership of the railways. I would like to appeal to the right hon. leader of the opposition, who I think, is quite in earnest when he says he is in favour of government ownership, that he use his best endeavours to see that the railways have a fair opportunity, that the management has a fair chance, and that at no time it may be said that any one in this House did anything that was not in the interests of all the people. It is absolutely necessary that these railways should prosper if Canada is to advance, as we hope it will, in the not far distant future.
Now, I want to speak very carefully. I listened attentively to the speech of the exMinister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton). With some of the remarks he made I am entirely in agreement. I have not yet had an opportunity to look carefully over the amendment he moved, but I agree with some of the ideas he expressed. Parliament cannot abdicate its authority or its responsibility in connection with these railways. The country has to make up the deficit of $50,000,000. Parliament is responsible to the people for the management of the railway, consequently I am not prepared to say that you can hand the whole thing over to a president and board of managers and say, "We are through with it; our responsibility is ended." The people of Canada will expect parliament to do its duty in this matter and to see that the operation of the railways is carried on efficiently. The people are the shareholders; they own the railway, and the elected members of this House are their representatives. How are we going to improve the existing
EMr. Forke.]
conditions? We have not yet solved the whole problem. The question we must face is, how shall the management be freed from galling and irritating interference by undue exposure of details of operation, and parliament still retain its authority? The House will understand what I mean when I ask the question:	How shall we keep the National
Railways out of partisan politics? That is the question we have before us to-day, and it is a question the country expects us to solve. The question is a difficult one. I do not wish to reflect upon any party in the House when I ask that question.
Some remarks have been made in connection with what occurred in 1920. I do not think we can compare conditions in 1920 with those that exist to-day. There was some trouble about management at that time; there had been no real consolidation of the different lines comprising what is now the Canadian National system. The old Canadian Northern was still on the boards to some extent, and the management of that day had not the opportunity, perhaps, of doing what can be done to-day with a consolidated system of railways and a board of management in complete control. I have read over the debates of 1921 and I think perhaps the then leader of the opposition, the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) made some remark at that time which he might well have left unsaid.
Words sometimes rise up as silent witnesses against us in the days to come, and consequently it behooves us at all times to be very careful what statements we make, more especially, I think, in the House of Commons, where our words are taken down and are always ready to bear silent witness to what our sentiments were in days gone by. However, I am not going to enter into that at the present time. I think that an attempt was made then to get information and particulars that it might not have been in the very best interests of the railway to give to the House at that time. I am not perfectly sure, Mr. Speaker, that political considerations did not enter into some of the work of this government at its inception, when it created. the board of directors for the Canadian National Railways. I am not making any charge, but I would not exactly put it past the government that they might do such a thing under certain circumstances. However, I believe that the appointment of Sir Henry Thornton and of the two Ministers of Railways who have been in charge under this government have saved the situation. I think every one of us who remembers the late Minister of Railways knows, that he was an upright and

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
able man, and that he gave the railways every chance that it was possible to give them. I would like also to pay this tribute to the present Minister of Railways:	I think he is
absolutely doing his best to see that the railways are a success, and that the board of management is allowed to carry on under the very best of conditions. But I would like to ask him, what of the future? I am not very sure whether the amendment that has been -moved in the House this afternoon will solve the problem or not. I am going to quote a few words that Sir George Foster used in 1921:
Members of parliament of both sides should get together and try and find a solution for the situation lying immediately in front of us. Let bygones be bygones for the time being, and let us approach at least this one question with a desire to get at the roots of the question, better still to find some sensible method of solving the problem.
We should get together. The ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) has gone out of the House, but I would like to make this proposition to him, that one member representing this party in the House, one member representing -his party, and another member representing the government, should get together and try to draw up this amendment so that it will be possible for all parties in the House to subscribe to it. That is what I call getting together, and that is not playing politics either. A committee of parliament, with the same powers as a committee of this House in connection with public accounts, it seems to me, might go just a little too far. On the other hand, a standing committee of the House, or a committee of the House, appointed to sit in consultation with the president and the board of the Canadian National Railways and discuss the whole problem, and advise and consult, X think may be the very best thing we could possibly have-something of that kind. I do believe, Mr. Speaker, that a committee that would be of an inquisitorial character, that would summon witnesses and put the president and members of the board on oath and take evidence, would not be in the interests of the country or of tfhe Canadian National Railways. Consequently, while I am in favour of parliament taking its responsibility and trying to solve this problem, of retaining to some extent its control of Canadian National affairs, and of being in a position to get information upon which it can form an intelligent opinion as to how the business of the railways is being carried on, I want to be very careful to see just what sort of a committee that may be. So I am not prepared at the present time to state without reservation that I would be in favour of appointing a select committee to go into all matters of detail in connection with the management of the railway.
This -is the position we find ourselves in at the present time. I repeat, I do not believe we have solved the problem when we simply say:	We will appoint a board of directors,
and hand over the management of the railways to them, leaving them entirely in their charge; because parliament must have control, must be responsible, and must in some way come in contact with that board. On the other hand, I am not prepared to see a committee appointed with full powers to call up the members of the board and investigate, and sit as a court of inquiry. I can see perfectly well how such a committee could work great damage by bringing to light and exposing a great many things that had better be left out of sight. I would like to have been able to suggest something helpful. Possibly a 'body of men or a committee could be found that would have an entirely different aspect from just a straight committee of the House. I make this suggestion quite respectfully. I know very well that I am not solving the question, but I realize the difficulties, and I want to go at -this thing very carefully, because I do believe that some such remedy may be found. I noticed an article in the Manitoba Free Press the other day, in which it made plain the difficulties, but it ended up very lamely by stating that it was up to parliament to find some solution of the problem. I do not know, Mr. Speaker, if I am doing any better. I am only stating the difficulties of the situation. But I am not sure that the ex-Minister of Finance, either, has solved the situation. I want time.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
Excuse me, I did not Bay
"perfect"; there is no such thing as perfection in this world. I should not like to see any such committee hampered in any way by partisan control. If we had a committee of that kind to-day the majority would probably be in the hands of the government, they would have to have a majority there. Well, I am not prepared to give the government a majority on such a committee to proceed simply as they saw fit. I think, perhaps, an intermediary body can be organized to act between parliament and the management of the Canadian National Railways. I believe in the patriotism of hon. members. I do not for one moment believe that any

party here would openly-and shall I say with malice aforethought?-do anything that would endanger the best interests of the Canadian National Railways. It seems to me that we know what our weaknesses are and we know what would happen in the event of action being taken along the lines proposed. I am not prepared-at this time anyway- to place power in the hands of any committee to go to any length it desires in investigating the affairs of the National system. This is a tremendous question and we should ponder carefully every step we take. What proposition did Sir George Foster have in his mind when he asked that the three parties in this House should get together and formulate some plan? He did not mean a standing committee, and he did not outline any simple plan which would be free from the difficulties of which I have spoken. However, it is possible that something may be done by mutual co-operation to help in the solution of this problem.
There is one matter in connection with the railways that I should like to mention- in fact it has been mentioned almost every time the Canadian National Railways have been spoken of-and that is the writing down of the capitalization of these railways. There is no doubt that vast sums of money have been spent on them, and spent not in the best ways, and it is equally true that the system is tremendously over-capitalized at the present time. It seems to me that it would be greatly to the advantage of all concerned if the capitalization was written down to something like the actual value of the railways at the present time. It would be an encouragement to the president of the system and1 to the board of management, it would also be something that the people at large would be proud of, if we were able to show, a surplus in operating revenue over expenses based on the actual value of the system. The people to-day are meeting large deficits. It is certain the deficit to-day is approximately fifty million, and the people have to make that good. Hence it would be to the advantage of all concerned if these railways were capitalized at something like their actual value.
I should also like to say a few words as to the character of the management. The esprit de corps of the railway employees, as I view it at the present time,-is of the very best. I think Sir Henry Thornton ought to be congratulated upon the excellent management, and upon the spirit of good will and service which seems to prevail among all the employees of the National system. I think

C.N.R.-Ministers Statement
every one must be struck with the courtesy, attention, and service one gets when travelling on the Canadian National Railways at the present time. This is equally true of the Canadian Pacific Railway. We get good service from our railroads but it must be remembered that we pay sweetly for it.
I shall not take up any time in dealing with the Scribe hotel. I am willing to leave in the hands of the government the issue which has been raised by the ex-Minister of Finance. It is a difficult question, one that I am not capable of discussing with any closeness of detail. It is possible that in the distant future it may turn out to be a very good investment, but it seems to me, from the information we have been able to obtain, that if the management had hastened a little more slowly in connection with the acquisition of this property it would have been better in the long run.
I do not think there is anything more to add. I am afraid I have not done very much towards solving the problem of getting into closer connection with the management of the Canadian National Railways but I would repeat this statement:	It would be unfortunate if any committee of this House were to be made an inquisitional body with power to examine into all the details of the management of the railway system. At the same time I should like to see a committee that would be a sort of advisory council, a committee with whom the managers of the railway could discuss the affairs of the National system.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
There are a few observations I
should like to make in regard to the statement of the Minister of Railways. I think it is hardly necessary to say that all sections of this House seem to be in favour of the principle of public ownership. But when it comes to our own National Railways system I always feel that we should keep clearly in mind that after all, to a considerable extent, the bondholders are the real owners of these railways. Holding the mortgages as they do they benefit more largely than the people generally have hitherto done.
Further, I think, we should not forget that whilst we advocate the principle of public ownership the effort must be to make public all the utilities and not a part of them. We must remember that side by side with our National lines we have the great rival system of the Canadian Pacific; and it is an open question whether or not operating our own National railways we can hope for success when there is another and rival system, both
companies operating in a comparatively limited field. I never go from here to Winnipeg, or from here to Montreal or Toronto, without recognizing the absurdity of having two lines paralleling one another so closely, and both pretty much on a parity as to their physical equipment and their service, without recognizing that we are facing a very serious question and one that must ultimately be decided by the people of Canada. However, I know that it is of no use talking about adding more burdens at the present time. We must ultimately however devise some plan to relieve ourselves of the burdens which we have assumed under the existing wasteful system.
Further than that, I would emphasize that while labour stands up for public ownership it also stands very decidedly for democratic control. The Minister of Railways in closing his statement made an appeal for fair dealing for the Canadian National Railways. He asked that the same freedom should be guaranteed to the officials as is accorded to those of private corporations. This would rather take for granted that the system of private corporations is an ideal one, and that I could not admit. Private corporations are organized from the top down, they are autocratic in their form of management; and anyone who has given any attention whatever to great industrial problems must recognize very clearly that the present system is not one which lends itself to the expression of the very best there is in the employees. It is quite true that autocracy in industry may mean a certain measure of efficiency, that claim is often made; and yet without co-operative effort it surely is impossible to have the very highest degree of efficiency.
I should like to pay the tribute to Sir Henry Thornton that he has done much to improve the morale, of the system. I have talked to many employees and I think they are honestly trying to do their very best under the circumstances to make the system efficient. They are proud of our Canadian National Railways. It appeals to an ideal that they have had for many years, and they hope that it is only in the process of a still further development. However, they are not altogether satisfied with existing arrangements. As you all know, the railway men's organizations on this continent have tried for some years to introduce a more democratic management into the conduct of the railroads. In the United States they have put forward the Plumb plan by which the management would represent the various interests that had to do with the railways, the officials, the employees on the road and in the shops, and the general public.

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
That plan has never been actually put into operation, and yet it represents an ideal towards which we are bound to strive. In Great Britain there was put forward a few years ago a plan somewhat similar, known as the Whitley plan. The present government a few years ago said a good deal wtih regard to the adoption of some such plan as that in Canada, and in fact we have the Labour department setting aside a certain estimate for the promotion of co-operative management between employer and employee. Why should we not begin that scheme in connection with our National Railways?

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
When the House
rose at six o'clock I was calling attention to the necessity of having not only public ownership but also, in order to ensure the success of that policy, some form of democracy in the management of our public institutions. I mentioned the Plumb plan which has been advocated by some railway men's organizations in the United States and also the scheme of Whitley councils which has been put forward in Great Britain. It is not my intention to-night to discuss these schemes or their merits but rather to urge the general principle that labour should be represented in industry, and more especially that this principle should be adopted in the public domain. In this I am advocating nothing new. I have in my hand a copy of a very well known document, Liberals and Labour issued in 1921. It was at that time resolved, and put forth as indicating the position of the Liberal party:
That the introduction into the government of industry of principles of repres&itation whereby labour and the community as well as capital may be represented in industrial control and their interests safeguarded and promoted in the shaping of industrial policies...
I take it that the idea behind this resolution distinctly was that even in private concerns labour should have its part in the control of industry. And if that was true of private concerns how much more important is it that the principle should be carried out in connection with our governmental institutions. I know it may be said that there is a labour man on the board of the Canadian National Railways. I have no objection to offer with regard to that particular individual;
I would point out however that he is not the chosen representative of labour; he is not in a direct sense the representative of the railway [Mr. Woodsworth.J
employees, and the whole idea behind the Whitley councils and other schemes of this character is that the employees should have their own representatives chosen by themselves. This same principle applies not merely in the railway service but in the Civil Service as well; for I may point out that it has been very frankly recognized in the Malcolm report of the committee which sat last year to investigate the Civil Service. I quote:
In the rapid growth of industry, great efficiency has
developed, but those charged with the problems of organization and management have found that this could only be accomplished by securing the greatest co-operation of their employees. The war emphasized this essential factor. As a result there have been established in private enterprises many forms of industrial councils which give representation to the employee on questions affecting his welfare. The need in private enterprise for some plan of employee representation finds its counterpart in a similar demand from those engaged in the public service.
Your committee has heard much valuable evidence on this subject; such plans as the Whitley councils have been presented as giving to the civil servant a voice in the settlement of problems affecting his welfare. Your committee, however, is unable, by reason of the diversity of evidence submitted, to recommend the acceptance of any definite plan now in existence as being adaptable to the conditions existing in this country under the present Oivil Service Act.
After reviewing the evidence and considering the problem from its various angles, your committee is impressed, however, with the necessity for the creation of some type of board on which the civil servant shall be represented so that the causes of complaint may be given fair consideration by those familiar with conditions in the service.
Your committee therefore recommends that the Civil Service Commissioners be given power to establish without delay departmental personnel boards to be made up of an equal representation of the Civil Service Commission, the department, and departmental employees. These boards are to act in an advisory capacity in matters of classification, promotion, dismissal, salary revision, leave of absence, and other kindred problems affecting the welfare and efficiency of the departmental service.
There the principle is very frankly recognized by the committee. I do not know why the government has not yet adopted that recommendation. I would urge that the same principle ought to find a place in the railway administration. We heard from the report the other day that Sir Henry Thornton had arranged radio stations so that he might address the employees all over the system.
I have not heard that any provision has been made for the establishment of a receiving station that he might hear what the employees have to say about the system. This might perhaps be considered as necessary as that he should speak to the employees.
The leader of the opposition in his criticism of the bookkeeping part of the report called attention to the fact that the freight

C.N.R.-Mmister's Statement
car repairs were less than in the previous year, that, however, there were heavy expenditures in new equipment, and that in this way charges of operation might possibly be cut, but on the other hand capital expenditure had been increased. This criticism I have had corroborated by some of those who are working very closely in connection with the repair operations on the railway.
I would suggest-
