speechtext:
I know nothing
whatever in regard to the latter statement. With respect to the former, as I said, I have had statements from some of those very closely connected with the repair work, and I can merely pass on what they have said to me in this matter.
I was going to call attention to some of the social effects of the closing down of the Canadian National and of the Canadian Pacific shops for considerable periods. This has meant an immense amount of unemployment and also a decrease in the purchasing power of the men, which has helped to further aggravate the business depression which has taken place at least in some parts of the country. In this connection I should like to call attention for a moment to some of the low wages paid on the Canadian National Railways. We have adopted in most of our public works the. principle of a fair wage. Certain classes of employees on the Canadian National Railways have been paid as low as 25 cents an hour. It has been stated that these are temporary employees. I should think that if men have to be employed for only short periods, that is all the more reason why the wage should be a fair wage; indeed it would seem a good reason why the wage should be higher than for men employed the year around. Here is a communication that will illustrate the feeling of some of the men in regard to this matter: The secretary of
the International Association of Machinists
writes me:
Track men and labourers reported to be receiving only $2 per day. If our information is correct, we ask if in your opinion it is possible for a man to exist on such wages, particularly as there has been no corresponding reduction in the cost of living and as the amount previously received by these men is so much lower than the cost of living figures as set out in the Labour Gazette, and which are understood to be the least that a man can live on. We think the management of the Canadian National Railways are very much ill-advised and are not working to the best interests of the country in reducing the standard of so many of their employees. It is such actions as these that have caused so many Canadians to migrate to the United States to secure employment at a decent living wage, and it is owing to the continuation of 6uch a policy on the part of the business interests of the country that Canada is so far behind the United States.
Surely the time has eome when we all recognize that a fair wage is decidedly in the interests of efficiency. More than that, looked at from the standpoint of society at large, about the only way by which we can hope to have the wheels of industry revolve more rapidly than at present is that there be an access of buying power. This is possible only as men receive more in the way of wages or services. Surely the business men of this country must have got away from some of the fallacies of economics and must recognize that it is only as the labouring men have money in their pockets that business men will prosper. Let me give one other example of the low wages paid in some departments of the National Railways. My correspondent, writing from a railway centre in Ontario, makes this statement:
I am forwarding jrou the time worked and the rate of pay paid by government railways to their employees in station restaurants. Time worked is twelve hours, 365 days per year, and in the event of taking a holiday, which you would think you would be entitled to after a year or two of service, they deduct pay for same. A manager and his wife are pa/id at the rate of $62.50 each per month; night help at the rate of $55 per month; kitchen help, $40 per month, all including board and room. For this large sum the manager has to secure a bond, to take all responsibility, and as you see, by working it out, hours worked for salary received amount to a very few cents per hour-

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
I do not wish to interrupt the hon. member, but it seems to me he should come closer to the subject matter of the amendment before the House. This amendment asks for the appointment of "a select standing committee on National Railways and Shipping to consider the estimates for the Canadian National Railway system and all questions involving new capital commitments and the disposition of properties and assets.''' Although the question which he raises is in some respects germane to the administration of the Canadian National Railway system, I do not think this is the proper

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
time for him to dwell on it. However, if he is coming closer to the amendment I have nothing further to say. I have merely interrupted him because I wish to recall not only to the hon. member himself but to all others who may speak on the amendment the following principle which will be found in Bourinot at page 421:
When an amendment has been moved to the question for the Speaker to leave the chair, discussion should be properly confined to its subject matter.
It is quite possible that the hon. gentleman is taking a roundabout way to come to the amendment. If so, very well; but so far I do not detect his intention to do that.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
I think I am travelling as fast as I can in the direction, Mr. Speaker, which you indicate. Since we are going into committee of Supply, and also since the amendment deals with the management of the railway and urges the appointment of a committee, I think I am quite in order in suggesting some of the things that would come before such a committee. However, I am through with that phase of the question and should like to come to a point that I think is clearly recognized in this House as being parliamentary in character.
We have been urged to keep the road out of partisan politics. I should like to ask how the road can be kept out of partisan politics so long as partisan politics are interwoven into the very structure of our parliamentary system. For example, in the appointment of the board of directors of the Canadian National, parliament as such has no voice; the appointment is made by the government. In other words it is made by a committee of the Liberal party, because after all the cabinet as it is now constituted is more or less a committee of the Liberal party. Parliament itself has no voice in the matter. Any amendment which we may offer from this side, under the present rules of the House, is regarded as a vote of want of confidence and the government's supporters are bound to try to defeat it. This arrangement, I submit, reduces the supporters of the government to silence and reduces us on this side to impotence. How can we bring about any change that is deemed desirable in the public interest in the management of the Canadian National? About the only thing we can do is to insist on the dismissal of the president. We do not want to do that. We can insist that the board be changed. We do not want to do that, and even if we did want to do it, the only way we could accomplish our purpose would be to turn out the government.

Surely we have to find some better machinery for carrying on this work if we hope that it will be kept out of partisan politics.
The fact is that the old party system of government grew up in an altogether different age, an age when the government was concerned largely in defence of the state and in managing the few concerns that were necessary, keeping up the roads, and that kind of thing. At that time there was no thought that a government would have to manage an enormous enterprise such as the Canadian National Railways, involving an expenditure of hundreds of millions of dollars. Under these circumstances it would seem as if the only way. we can possibly keep the road out of partisan politics is by rejecting some of the partisan machinery that exists and that impedes our progress.
Our problem essentially is how to maintain control over the expenditure and policy of the road-that we owe to our constituents- and at the same time how we may avoid partisan and non-technical interference in a highly technical business enterprise. We have attempted to do this by the rather awkward expedient of a commission. Those who insist on our doing things always in accordance with the old British constitutional practice will, I think, have to recognize fundamental changes when they consider these commissions that are being established. We have a number of them, the oustanding ones, of course, being the Railway Commission and the Civil Service Commission. The attempt has undoubtedly been to take these important branches of the service out of politics, but in effect the danger is that we set up in each case an independent body over which parliament has little if any control. Such a commission might very easily become absolutely autocratic in its policy. We have had mention to-day of the Scribe affair, an incident, I think, that no one can very well justify. We want not to embarrass the railways, not to embarrass the government in carrying on that enterprise, but rather to work out some sort of arrangement that will prevent such unfortunate incidents in the days to come.
I might mention another little incident that occurred last year. We spent several weeks in this House debating our immigration policy. The item directly under discussion related to the granting of a sum of money to the Canada Colonization Company. After we had spent weeks in debate we found that the Canadian National, without any debate in the House whatever, was also making a grant to the Canada Colonization Company. It did not make any difference whether we voted in favour or against; the fact was that we had

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
established another body that could absolutely undo the work of parliament-an independent body, the Canadian National Railway Board, that might carry out a certain immigration policy despite all that could be said in this House. A policy which grants such power to a few is intolerable.
Take the question of freight rates: With all the machinery we have-with the board of management, the Railway Commission and our Railway department-I wonder whether we have effective control over freight rates to-day? If I understand the matter rightly, freight rates are, at least in part, determined by a board upon considerations that affect directly our great rival in the railway business, the Canadian Pacific. Ho-w can we hope to do successful business through our Canadian National when one of the considerations that deterniine the rates charged is the effect of those rates upon a rival railroad? I have in mind, of course, certain freight rates through the mountains, over which our own road, built with easy grades, finds it difficult to ship the goods it might because of the probable effect upon the rival road, which has a much more difficult grade-so at least, it is stated. Some of these rates and arrangements, as we had illustrated to us last year, are decided by a board that is even international in its scope.
I do not know that our representative is actually a member of that board, but I believe he still sits in and listens to its deliberations, and the policy is undoubtedly affected. There is all along the line the danger that a board of this kind may become so independent as to be out of the control of the representatives of the people.
I would like to mention just in passing one or two matters of policy. We are carrying on an extensive business outside of the railway business-the maintenance of hotels, in connection with our tourist traffic. These hotels, we are told, are being run at a loss. It is a question how far we should subsidize great commercial institutions of this kind that minister to only one class in the community. The leader of the Progressives (Mr. Forke) this afternoon, mentioned the splendid dining and sleeping car service on the Canadian National, and I quite agree with him. But I should like to suggest that this service is maintained very largely for one class of the community. Last autumn I happened to come down from Winnipeg to Toronto on a train on which there were a large number of returning harvest hands. I noticed that all the way from Winnipeg to Toronto there were only [DOT] two restaurants at which these men
could obtain any sort of lunch. Two days on the road, and yet only two possible places at which they could purchase refreshments!
It was all very well for those who had the money to go into the dining car, but here we were maintaining an elaborate system designed for tourist traffic, and at the same time we were not supplying the needs of the men who were carrying on the productive industry of this country. It is all very well to have new inventions like the radio exploited, and we are very glad to think we are in the fore-front of that work, and yet while we have been supplying the needs of tourists patronizing sleeping cars and big hotels, I sometimes wonder whether it has not been done at the expense of some of those who must travel over the lines in less expensive cars or who, because they have to pay high freight rates, must put up at much less elaborate hostels.
With regard to the amendment itself, it would seem to me to look in the right direction. I have not had the opportunity of studying it clause by clause. The leader of the Progressives seems to fear something that, as I heard it read, was not in the text. He suggested a third intermediary body, but did not divulge to the House just exactly the character or powers of this third body.
I should say that the present board of management more or less fills the place which the leader of the Progressives had in mind. We need however a committee that really represents the rank and file of the people. As I listened to the member who proposed the amendment (Sir Henry Drayton) there occurred to me an idea that has come very frequently to my mind as I have sat here during the estimates. Why should not many of these estimates be discussed in small committees? We cannot possibly, in this large committee of the Whole understand all the details of all the different departments. The result is that a good many of us must seek refuge outside while these estimates concerning which we have no knowledge are being discussed. If we had half a dozen different committees working concurrently, it would seem to me we would save an immense amount of the time of this House and do much more effective work. In the committees we might have the deputy ministers or the various officials of the departments present, and then we would not need to have the immense strain of listening to the snappy sentences the minister gets from his deputy and then presents to the House. It would seem. then. too. as if we might dis'

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
pense with the Hansard for committee work, and we would not be induced to make speeches then as we are at the present time.

I am very glad
that the House appreciates that position, and I for one would be very glad to accommodate myself to the changed condition. Under such an arrangement the increasing business of this country could be carried on much more effectively.

speechtext: It would shorten the session too.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
Yes, it would shorten the session very decidedly. Mention was made of the safeguard the government has in having a majority on all committees. I would point out, in passing, that it is stated that in Great Britain the practice is to have the committees arranged so that the government does not have proportionately more representation in the committees than it has in the House. I do not know why that principle should not be adopted here. But let me ask, why should we constantly take it for granted that a committee, charged with the discussion of the conduct of our railway affairs, would try to block the progress or the development of our Canadian National Railways? Somebody says, as long as you have human nature you cannot do very much. Well I am sure most of us, if we think a little more deeply, will recognize that human nature is pretty good after all, if it only has a decent evironment and decent machinery with which to work. I feel confident that public sentiment is so much behind the Canadian National Railway system to-day that no section of the community would dare to do anything to break that system or to impair its efficiency.
Perhaps I should alter that statement a little because, as a matter of fact there are some sections of the community, certain interested sections, that appear to be trying to do that very thing, but I think that considering the Canadian people as a whole there is no section of the community that will effectively defy public opinion along this line. So it would seem as if we ought to have some such committee as has been suggested by the amendment. But, speaking for the group which I represent and, I think, for a very large number of the Canadian people across this country, I would say that there must be nothing done whatsoever that will jeopardize 
or impair the welfare of the Canadian National system; there must be no sabotaging of the railways or the marine. Given that as a starting point, as something we must all keep in mind, it would seem to be the wise thing to devise the machinery now by which we can more adequately administer the affairs of this great corporation.

subsubtopic: DISCUSSION OF ANNUAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to refer to one thing that the hon. member (Mr. Woodsworth) brought up, and that was he thought there ought to be an improvement in the way this House conducts its business. I would like to see the old committee that we had a year or two ago, called the Speaker's committee, revived, and the House in a very careful and well-thought out manner try to reorganize the conduct of its business so as to save time, expedite business, cut out a lot of speeches, and shorten the session.
To-night I want for a few minutes to discuss the Canadian National Railways, brought up by the Minister of Railways when he presented his report, and to discuss also the amendment. To begin with, to justify my position, and my position is to be a justification of public ownership of railways in this country, some years ago I favoured that position and I was laughed at, -but whether I was laughed at or not I lived to see public ownership of railways arrive in this country, and the people are satisfied with it; they are proud they own this railway, that it is theirs. Yet somebody wants to take it away from them. To show what the criticism is of the Canadian National Railways I am going to read just a line or two from a Montreal newspaper that reviewed the report as presented by the Minister of Railways a few days ago. The Montreal Gazette on last Friday said:
Our National Railway did fairly well last year. It made headway financially, but it cost the country $51,697,000. That is not quite as much as the sum derived from the income tax, but it more than suffices.
It has cost the people of Canada $290,000,000 to adventure upon public ownership, over and above a liability of $2,000,000,000. That is the plain fact. Was the experiment worth while? Results do not support an affirmative answer, nor yet does an analysis of the balance sheet.
And it says this is the test of public ownership. Where did we get this test of public ownership? It came from years of adventuring in railroad construction in this country, adventures in which an enormous amount of profiteering was done in connection with contracts. Unnecessary roads were built, unnecessary headquarters were started all over. We had three or four experiments.

C.N.R.-Ministers Statement
and they all lost money; not only these three or four experiments, but there were dozens of other lines established in this country, and they all had to be taken care of and were a burden on the people. Included in them is a railway which is probably the most expensively constructed of all, the Grand Trunk Pacific although its construction, in a way, has something to justify it. The Grand Trunk Pacific was built as an offset to the Canadian Pacific, and the latter was not constructed for nothing by the people of this country. It cost them twenty millions of money and twenty-five million acres of land, and there have been many other obligations since that time. Public ownership is derided, but what we are doing now is cleaning up the mess created by preceding administrations in parliament. An enormous amount of money has been put into these railroads but the Conservative administration had the courage to consolidate the Grand Trunk and all the lines the Grand Trunk had acquired in its early days; the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Canadian Northern, and all the other lines, into one system and take them over. The people took over these different roads, consolidated them into one system and put it under public ownership. That was done to clean up the mess that had been created in this country by private ownership. That was the cure that was adopted. And yet we see the taunt in the Montreal Gazette "Look at the mess you have got into from public ownership." Why, we are trying to remedy a condition which has prevailed in this country for forty years. Because we are trying to clean up that mess we are being denounced in the way I have indicated. The Liberal administration is also trying to clean up this mess, following the same lines as its predecessor. The opponents of public ownership do not say anything about that system where it was established on its merits.
If you want to talk to me about public ownership, if you want to throw stones at it, go to the province of Ontario and see what has been accomplished there in the way of hydro-electric distribution. That system is owned by the people. There has been no waste of money on it. There may have been a little money lost, and some mistakes may have been made, but it is the finest instance of public ownership in the world to-day. It is owned by the people of Ontario and they have an unlimited supply now of electrical energy for industry, for lighting and, to a limited extent, for heating their houses. They also have a fine system of electrical railways in connection with it. If the Montreal Gazette
would take that as an instance of public ownership it would be on fairer ground. What that paper is denouncing, as I have said before, is the horrible mess created by various parties, and by various adventurers in railway construction in this country.
Let me give you another instance of successful public ownership. The Toronto street railway is owned by the people and it is the finest system of its kind in America to-day. The fares of that system are going to come down, and the whole debt is being amortized. In about thirty years the debt will be all paid off. There are radial lines in connection with it, and they are proving a great success. The city of Detroit has acquired its street railway, and is going to give it the same treatment which has been bestowed by the people of Toronto on their railway.
These are only a few instances of the success of public ownership. There are others. What is the great feature in the report of the Dawes commission in connection with repatriation in Germany? The first condition laid down in that report for the recovery of Germany is that the national lines which did so much in the past for the development of that country, must be maintained. That is where Germany showed its strength years ago when she took over the railroad system and developed the country by means of national railways. Talking about the nationalization of railways, if I can read the signs of the times, the present government in England to-day-the Ramsay MacDonald government, a labour government-after dealing with the housing problem will undertake a nationalization of the railways there. As a result of the nationalization of the railways power will be distributed to all the industries in the country. They propose to establish great plants, equipped with batteries of steam boilers, which will develop enough energy to electrify their industries. They have not got water-power there but they have an abundance of coal.
Now, as to the United States. I am only a prophet, and perhaps a poor prophet, but I am convinced that it will not be long before a movement will be started to nationalize the railroads in that country. At present there is great dissatisfaction with the operation of the railways, and with other things. It will cost billions of dollars to take over the railways in the United States, but there is no other solution of existing difficulties but to do that. The railway brotherhoods may do something in that direction. There may possibly be an objection to the railway brotherhoods dictating too much in that connection, but I am not afraid of that. It may result in their

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
getting a better system of railroads than they ever had before, and I think they are prepared to try the experiment there. Then the United States government has practically given national leadership and national capital in connection with the banking system of that country. That is the kind of public ownership we are talking about here. You may abuse it, you may make fun of it and say it will never come about, but it has arrived. It has arrived in connection with the public affairs in the United States and in connection with the real leadership of banking over there. The capital behind this banking system is national money, and public money will go into the nationalization of railways over there. The province of Quebec has gone into banking to the extent of investing fifteen millions of public money.
The principle of public ownership is being asserted all over the world and is winning out, and yet we read in papers like the Montreal Gazette that public ownership is an abuse. I say it is not. I say that what we are engaged in is cleaning up the mess in connection with our railways, as a result of adventuring and of profiteering, and perhaps politicians were more or less involved in it. The Montreal Gazette is carrying on this campaign and for what purpose? I understand what is going on in the city of Montreal to-day, and I see it in other places not so very far away. I see the effort being made to compel the people of Canada to surrender the Canadian National Railways and to give them to the Canadian Pacific. That is the object of the attack that is being made in all quarters. Remember the National Railways are owned by the people and they are going to make the proposition a success. That is the object of the attack which is being made.
The Canadian National is owned by the people of Canada, but the Canadian Pacific Railway is owned outside of Canada, and the proposal of the Montreal Gazette is to give the traffic to the Canadian Pacific. A large portion of the stock of the Canadian Pacific Railway is held in the States, in England, and in Germany. We do not know where it is owned. We have a road of our own, which is beginning to pay and it runs from ocean to ocean. When I talk about abuses in regard to Canadian roads in the past, I do not say it was an abuse to build the Intercolonial road, but it cost a lot of money and is not paying its way to-day. But we have that road now. There was a political reason for building that road, and there was a more or less political reason for the building of the Grand Trunk Pacific and perhaps in connection with the construction of all the roads in the coun-
try. Our road is beginning to promise to pay; this government has followed the policy of the previous government fairly well, is voting money freely enough for the railways and does not seem to be interfering with the administration. There was no interference under the administration of the previous government. We have a great road costing two billion dollars, running from Halifax to Vancouver, with all the strategy of the continent compared with the Canadian Pacific Railway. The greatest road of them all is the Grand Trunk Pacific. All the strategy of Ontario, from a railway point of view, is owned by the National Railways, the old Grand Trunk. It is, to a large extent the same in Quebec and the Maritime provinces. This road connects all the ports of Canada, Vancouver, Prince Rupert and Victoria on the Pacific coast, with all the ports in the East. Its business is growing in every direction, and it will soon be selfsupporting.
When the board is appointed I think the first thing for parliament to do would be to fix a fair amount as the cost of the Canadian National Railways and say to those in charge of the road, "You must earn the interest on that amount and pay it." I believe that, under such a policy, we would be able to pay the national debt in a short time. But I will come to that later when we deal with the reconstruction of the Finance department. If we adopt that course the road will soon begin to pay.
The motive actuating Montreal in the attack on the National Railways is fear that the publicly owned roads, notwithstanding the burden handed down to them from the past, are going to win out, and Montreal does not like it. I am not saying one word against the Canadian Pacific Railway. They may not be at the bottom of it. It is the big English speaking interests who do not want to see the Canadian National Railways owned by the country. They do not want the hydro power in Ontario, but they would like to develop power on the St. Lawrence and I hope that some day the St. Lawrence will be consecrated to the electrification of the National Railways adjacent to them, and that when that electrification goes to the West and is developed there will be enough surplus power to take care of the household needs of the farmers of the West. Electrical development will help the Maritime provinces. If you want to see power developed in those provinces, take up the proposal to use the Bay of Fundy tide for electrical energy. It will work out all right, and is a good proposition. In that way we w^ould improve our country and build

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
up the National Railways. First of all, create a great system of power for the electrification of railways and share it with the people, as Ontario has shared its power with the people, and build up the National Railways and they will be a great success.
In regard to the management of the railways, my suggestion would be that you should appoint a commission of five of the highest class of railway men you could get, men like Sir Henry Thornton, Sir Henry Drayton, Mr. Beatty, Mr. Ruel and another man who has had some experience. Those five men could run the road and make it the greatest national road in the world, and it could be done better by five men than in any other way. I would not like to take the control of the railway away from parliament; but I would leave it to five men to run the road from ocean to ocean, give them big pay as commissioners to manage the affairs of the road, and prohibit them from bringing politics into it. Pick out the best men, and the result would be that we would have the greatest example to the world of public ownership of railways. We can adopt this scheme in this country, as we have the men to do it. For a while, I did think that progress would result if we had a consolidation of the Canadian Pacific with the Canadian National; but possibly the people of the West favour opposition in connection with railways; they want the two systems. I cannot make the suggestion just now that the Canadian Pacific should come in; but if the management of that road adopt the tactics which have been adopted in the past, to destroy the Canadian National, the management had better think twice before going much further with that programme. That is what they are doing at Montreaband at other places, and you can see the slimy trail wherever you go.
It may not be in the public interest to consolidate; but if the Canadian Pacific Railway is wise, the management will approach the government and the people of Canada and say "We have enormous resources yet, but we think they belong to the shareholders and we propose to distribute them". I do not know that they belong to the shareholders altogether. When Sir John A. Macdonald created the Canadian Pacific Railway he inserted a clause in the charter that nobody was quite able to understand, to the effect that the road was to be maintained forever. For what? That requires interpretation. I say the road was built for the benefit of the people of Canada in connection with transportation. The Canadian Pacific directors have successfully administered their road, and 172

I give them credit for it; but Sir John A. Macdonald, when he started that road, and Sir Wilfrid Laurier when he projected the Grand Trunk Pacific, did not say that union was not strength. The day may come when union will be strength in the case of the railways. If the Canadian Pacific comes in they can get a fair division of profits on their investment, and they may have certain assets they can distribute; but if they want to do something to help public ownership in this country, let them first come to the country and make a proposition. They might say, "We do not see why we should maintain the railway end of it, but we are willing to maintain the steamship end of it". There would be a chance then for the Canadian Pacific if they wanted to handle the transportation of the country. Let them go into the steamship business and the settlement of the country, on some understanding with the people of Canada and in that way they will go ahead. I say that there is a conspiracy and that the head of it is in the Mount Royal Club in Montreal.
Order, order.

I do not say the club proper, but there is a bloc in Montreal which would like to destroy the National Railways, and destroy Ontario as far as the distribution of power is concerned. They would also like to smash Toronto because that city owns the street railway. But other cities are going the same way. I am not an enemy of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and. I give them every credit; but there is room for the Canadian National Railways as well as the Canadian Pacific. The 9 p.m. Canadian National Railways in the estimation of the people is their own road and the people are proud that they own the system, notwithstanding the debt which they owe in connection with it. I come in contact with the public frequently and I know that the people are patronizing the National Railways more than they have ever done before. It is not wise I say for the Canadian Pacific, through the medium of its directors, the newspapers and its friends, to insinuate that the Canadian people cannot manage their own railways and therefore ought to turn them over to that company. There are very few public men in Canada who venture to take that position, although there are some who apparently would like to have the Canadian National Railways handed over to the Canadian Pacific. That is not my idea, and I am sure that my constituents are stoutly in support of public ownership.

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
I have been in public life for thirty years and have always believed in and advocated the principle of public ownership, and thank God I am alive to-day to see that principle vindicated. I repeat, the people of Canada are proud of the railways they own; and I challenge those men who try to detract from the success of the system to come out into the open and attack it. I invite any opponent of the National Railways to come into my riding and discuss the question freely; and I on my part am prepared to go into any province in the Dominion, either in the East or in western Canada, and meet squarely on any platform any one who is attacking the railways in an unfair or an irresponsible way. It is high time that these people were warned, and I believe that if proper steps were taken to put the matter fairly before the country, those who are trying to subvert public ownership would cease from their attacks on the National Railways. At any rate, let the opponents of the system come out in the open and fight. I know very little about the West, but I am ready to risk my chances of success on any platform there in defence of public ownership. It is time that the Canadian Pacific Railway abandoned their scheming and their insinuating that the Canadian National system cannot be properly managed by the people. The Canadian Pacific Railway simply wants to get hold of the system, and if it did it would be master of the country. What hope would there be for politics in this country if a privately owned company, controlled in the United States, in Great Britain and in Germany, should take over the National Railways? Why, the men in Montreal have no more power over the Canadian Pacific Railway to-day than they can derive from their shareholders; and the majority of the shareholders of the company live outside of Canada.
I have been watching events in the United States and I know that the greatest company ever formed anywhere in the world is being floated to-day in New York to monopolise public utilities; in this enterprise there are associated the Bell Telephone Company and the American Telegraph & Telephone together with cable concerns and the Marconi people. They are capitalising at one billion or two billion dollars and they will simply control all communications both at home and in Europe. Now, I think it would be much -better for us in this country if we went in for some enterprise that would extend our own activities; we have a good telegraph system and can connect up with the world. And there are many other ways in which we could develop our utilities.

Some people of the United States look with dread upon what is going on in Canada in connection with our National Railways, because the American roads are unable to make any headway themselves, having been overcapitalized. Some two years before his death President Harding was approached by prominent railway men in the United States in connection with the railway situation there, and at that time he expressed the view that if they would partition the railway systems of the United States into ten regional divisions they would be able to secure enough money from the government to electrify the roads and consolidate them. That would have made their railways stronger than ever; but they have not succeeded. There is the greatest jealousy on the part of the railway concerns over there of public ownership in Canada; and notwithstanding the difficulties with which the system here has had to contend, I think I may say that we have lower traffic rates here than there are in any other country. And this because parliament has kept control of the rates. Apart from a return of 3 or 4 per cent on investments, all other earnings will go towards a reduction in railway rates; and the secret of public ownership is to give service at the lowest cost and not merely to put money into the pockets of shareholders. I think the people of Canada, as time goes on, will find the Canadian National Railway system the greatest boon. At present the people of the West have a good deal to worry about; they have had a hard time on their farms and have had many grievances. I hope therefore that the government will find some way to extend the farm credit system in the West. But the one thing that would do most for western Canada would be a reduction in railway rates, and the only way in which railway rates can be reduced is for the Canadian National Railway system, through proper management, to take the initiative in this direction and to make the Canadian Pacific march at the same pace.
In the past forty years we have had a good deal of profiteering and political adventuring in this country in connection with the railways; but that is not public ownership. I have no doubt whatever that public ownership can be and will be successful in this country, and I want to see it given a fair show. If this is to be brought about politics must be eliminated. Of course, I want parliament to be ultimately responsible for the administration of the railways; parliament must see to it that proper men are put in charge of them and are given adequate assistance by means

C.N.R.-Minister s Statement
of the necessary legislation. But apart from that the railways should be left to the administration of the men whose services are devoted to their management, men who are not in politics. It is true that charges of extravagant expenditures may be brought; but these things have happened in connection with other concerns. And the Canadian Pacific Railway has not such an unenviable record itself. It did not cost an awful lot, and it has been handled well. But I should like to see the Canadian Pacific Railway subject to an inquisition in this parliament; they would then be just as eager to protect their reputation as anybody else. I want to give a warning to the Mount Royal Club, as I call them, and the big interests who are associated with them, who hate public ownership and power distribution, and who want to grab the St. Lawrence and the Ottawa water-power. I hope that we shall develop the water-power of the St. Lawrence, because we can levy an export duty on that power going out of the country. But the Montreal men want to export it to the United States; they want to smash the Canadian National Railways and then get control of them.

Will my hon. friend allow
me a question?
Yes, two.

Will he be more explicit?
He says that Montreal wants to export power to the United States. Who is "Montreal"?

They have two
propositions now. You will see them come before us this session.
Who are "they"?
They are developing the Lachine-
Will the hon. member explain who "they" are?

I will rise in my
place and name some of the parties. I thought all our friends outside of Montreal, our Quebec friends, were very much in favour of public ownership of railways and waterpower.
You know I never was.

Not in favour
of National Railways?

I was never in favour of
public ownership.

But you have
got to do with it to-day. Are you ashamed of it? After the mess that we are trying to
172$
clean up, that awful mess which nobody can clean up to-day but the people of Canada- that is what I am saying-is my hon. friend ashamed of that mess?

My hon. friend asked me
if I was in favour of public ownership. I told him, no. I always said so in this House.

Then you are
not in sympathy with your party?
You are from Montreal.

I am not from Montreal.
I can think for myself; I am not following the band wagon with the crowd.
I hope the government will stand up and justify public ownership. If so, surely all the members of the government must Stand for it.
I will stand for it and help it, but I do not believe in it.

Perhaps my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) may not agree with his colleague. If I could gather anything from the most excellent speech which the Minister of Justice delivered the other day it was this-he was telling the people of Canada and this House that the mantle of Sir Wilfrid had fallen on him. I hope he is not ashamed of having made that statement. It is to his credit that he said so. Sir Wilfrid Laurier at great risk undertook the building of the Grand Trunk Pacific, which is the greatest railway in the world, and I give him credit for its construction. It carries the majority of the passengers in the West, it carries the grain of most of the wheat fields of the West, and the development of water-power in connection with it will help to electrify all the western provinces.
I am not objecting to the motion very much, but I take this opportunity-and I am only a weak voice in this House-to serve notice on the Canadian Pacific that if it is their object to wipe out the National Railways, they had' better come before the people of Canada and openly declare that to be their intention. Let them go on the platform in the province of Ontario or in any other of the provinces and tell the people: "We want you to give us these National Railways. We will run them and make a success of them." Let them say that openly to the people, and they will find that neither the people nor the newspapers of this country will justify them in that declaration. I can see some queer aids, from the newspaper point of view, coming to the Montreal Gazette

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
these, days. Those aids are coming not from the usual quarters but from the province of Ontario in an attempt to smash the National Railways. Let them come out in the open and say that that is their object, and they will get the worst smashing that any party ever got in this country Let any party, I do not care which it may be, try surreptitiously to destroy the National Railways, and in this House or in any part of Ontario I shall be willing to meet any such friends of the Canadian Pacific, and they will find themselves smashed instead of their smashing the National Railways.
Mr. FRANK S. CAHILL (Pontiac):	Mr. Speaker, I feel that the government is to be congratulated on their good fortune in being able to present such a satisfactory report of the Canadian National Railway system for the past year. The report shows that the net earnings are better by $17,000,000 than they were last year. The gross earnings increased by $20,000,000, while those of the Canadian Pacific Railway increased by only $9,000,000. The net earnings of the Canadian Pacific increased by only $1,170,000, while the net earnings of the Canadian National increased by $17,349,000. It has been suggested that a part of this increase is due to the skimping of expenditures on maintenance of way and maintenance of equipment, but I find on looking over the Canadian Pacific report for 1922 that the Canadian National spent more per mile of railway than the Canadian Pacific did. So if the Canadian National spent a little less last year for maintenance of way and maintenance of equipment they are still spending more, than the Canadian Pacific in this respect. Therefore the showing is really very satisfactory from the standpoint of the government. Apparently the government were very fortunate in securing the services of Sir Henry Thornton as president of the system. He came here only a little over a year ago, but I think before he had landed he was attacked by the leader of the opposition. I do not remember on what ground, but I think that in a by-election which was then being held the right hon. gentleman was reported as having attacked Sir Henry Thornton. Apparently it was his intention to give the National Railways a chance by trying to condemn the president before he had taken over the job!
The mover of the amendment, my hon. friend from West York (Sir Henry Drayton), started out by saying that he was in favour of the Canadian National Railway system and wanted to do everything he could to assist in its development and betterment,

but he wound up by calling the present board of directors political hacks or political heelers. I do not know just how much of this a member is supposed to believe. I know a member's word must be accepted, but I hope we do not have to believe the whole of his statement. By describing the directorate as political hacks, in what way could he help the Canadian National Railways or the government? He must have had one of two objects in view, either to condemn the government or to condemn the railway management. If he is in favour of the Canadian National Railways-and he himself states that he is in favour of public ownership, which is going further than many members in this House would care to go- how can he hope to assist the Canadian National management by condemning the directorate? With some of his opening statements I agree, but with most of those which he uttered during the last hour and a half of his speech I must disagree. He indicated at the outset that it might be possible to have a commission or a board of management appointed which would be more continuous in office than under the present system. He attempted to condemn the government for changing the old directorate, but he intimated1 that if he were a member of the next administration he would take the same course and dismiss the present directorate. If this be the case, then there might be something in his suggestion that a commission should be appointed which would continue in office even after a change of government. It might bring about more continuity of management and be more satisfactory to the officials of the road. But he did not propose that to the House; he wound up by moving an amendment asking for a committee of the House to go into the details of the expenditures and the management of the system. A committee was appointed during the last parliament with powers somewhat similar, perhaps a little more restricted. We of the opposition contended for the committee and the government contended against it. We finally got a committee with restricted powers, and for myself I think the committee was of very little service.
I do not know what the government's intention is with regard to this amendment, but it does not seem to me that it is going to solve the whole problem of Canadian National Railway management. The hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton), in arguing in favour of his amendment, intimated that he was anxious to get to the bottom of certain things. He proposed practically to have an inquisition of the Canadian National manage-

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
ment and to have the officials of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company conduct that inquisition; that is about what his amendment means. I do not know that any good purpose can be served by such a committee or by such an inquisition. I do feel, as I have always felt, that everything pertaining to the management and operation of the National Railways should be public property. After all, the people are responsible for the obligation; they are responsible for the expenditures.
It has been suggested by the Manitoba Free Press and by some hon. members that some kind of committee or body should be organized for the purpose of taking the management of the road out of politics, but I think the argument will not bear close analysis. Under our system of government, under any system of government, the government business must be conducted by the government, call it political or partisan or whatever you will. If you try to eliminate government influence then you have to establish another body which will have control of the railway system. They in turn would have to find the money to provide for the deficit. Where would they get that money? Either by the power being conferred upon them to impose taxation on the people, or by their coming to parliament; so that it gets back eventually to the same thing.
The government of the day argued, on the occasion to which I referred a moment ago, that the railways were to be kept out of politics, that the directorate was to be a nonpolitical body; but we of the opposition contended, as my hon. friends opposite are contending now, that that would be impossible. So the thing got into the position it is in today without very much thought on the part of the government of the day or on the part of the advocates of public ownership of that day. The government now have to deal with it.
They have been fortunate in securing a manager who has been able to show a very great betterment in the condition of the road. It may not be Sir Henry Thornton, I do not know. He may not be a railroad man, but if he is not he was very fortunate in coming in at a time when the improvement was as great as it has been in the last year. The Canadian people will be inclined to believe that he is responsible for a great part of that betterment, if not all of it; they will be inclined to believe that there must be some influence that has brought about a betterment greater than that achieved by the Canadian Pacific. I think it is not altogether due to the change in government, although that m"st have quite a lot to do with it.
The hon. member for West York also proposed in his amendment that all questions involving new capital commitments and the disposition of properties and assets should be dealt with by this committee. I did not like to interrupt him while he was speaking, but I felt like asking him, and hoped he would be in his seat now that I might ask him, just what he meant by that. Did he mean that the Canadian National management would not be permitted to sell lands, for instance, townsites, timber, or any of the properties that they must sell from time to time? Or did he mean that they were not to be allowed to sell a portion of the railway? Just what did he mean, if he meant anything? Or did that portion of his amendment mean about as much as the rest of it-that he merely wants to be able to bring in the Canadian Pacific management to hold an inquisition and to show up the weaknesses, if any, of the Canadian National Railways, and to let the Canadian Pacific go away scot free?
If the Canadian Pacific officials consent to come before a committee of parliament to give information against the Canadian National Railways, I may say to my hon. friend who moved the amendment that the Canadian Pacific is badly advised. If the members of the opposition who are apparently championing the Canadian Pacific wish to make a contest between the people of Canada and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company or between the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, I have no hesitation in saying that the Canadian Pacific is likely to get the worst of it. I do not believe the Canadian Pacific wants to enter into a contest of that kind. I would be glad to see the Canadian National Rail-mays managed as well as the Canadian Pacific has been managed in the past. I would like to see them have an equal chance. But from some indications appearing in the Railway committee it would seem that a number of the advocates of the Canadian Pacific are inclined to favour that railroad as against the Canadian National The number is small, but apparently there are those who wish to do that. Legislation was held up last year in regard to branch lines, and we saw instances in the Railway committee where the Canadian Pacific had practically gone over the same territory, had constructed lines of railway that the Canadian National had intended to construct. A remark was made in the press a few days ago to the effect that one of the members of the committee had suggested a change in the destination of one of the Canadian National branch lines. Yes, he suggested that, but the Canadian National management

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
had asked for identically the same line the year before and it had been refused by parliament. The Canadian Pacific in the meantime went in and built the line, so, that the change of destination did not mean very much because the Canadian National could not build on top of the Canadian Pacific. So I want to say to my hon. friend from West York that his advocacy of the Canadian National Railways will not only be detrimental to the Canadian National but will also be very detrimental to the Canadian Pacific.
Mr. Speaker, I do not like to interrupt the hon. member, but he has absolutely not the slightest justification for his statement.

Did my hon. friend not say this afternoon that he wished to have a committee to investigate the affairs of the Canadian National? Did he not also say that he wished to have a committee before which he could bring the Canadian Pacific officials?

What I said was very clear. I said that from the file brought down and from the information I had, it would appear that a fraud was being perpetrated on the Canadian people, and that if that property had been offered to the Canadian Pacific for $1,400,000, then we should know it. I said nothing whatever as to aiding the Canadian Pacific, one way or the other. The hon. gentleman, I think, was not in the House.

Yes, Mr. Speaker, I was
in the House and heard the hon. member distinctly-
That makes it worse.

*-make the statement that he hoped to bring the Canadian Pacific officials here to prove his allegations, that and nothing else. He let the cat out of the bag with regard to this committee that he is proposing; he is going to bring the Canadian Pacific officials here to hold an inquisition on the Canadian National Railway management; it was either that or nothing at all.
To find out the truth, whether the property was in the market.
Where did my hon. friend get his information?
I have not got it; I want to get it.

Then in making his statements he is just guessing, to the detriment of the Canadian National Railways. Does he think he is enhancing the reputation of Sir Henry Thornton by coming here and insinuating that he has paid very much more for the Hotel Scribe than the Canadian Pacific could have bought it for? Does he think that is helping the management? Does he think he is helping the management of the Canadian National Railways when he says the directors are political hacks? Is that helping to promote the welfare of the Canadian National Railways?
That is known, unfortunately.

My hon. friend says that is known. The only purpose my hon. friend can have in mind must be the making of political capital, and if he is attempting to make political capital he cannot be helping the Canadian National Railways. If he will come into my province and make that statement about an ex-member of this House from my province, I can tell him that he will not gain any votes in the province of Quebec, and I think the same will apply to the other directors throughout the country.
I would like to ask what my hon. friend means by one portion of his amendment. The amendment reads:
That a select standing committee on National Railways and Shipping is hereby appointed, to consider the estimates for the Canadian National Railway system and the Mercantile Marine, and all questions involving new capital commitments and the disposition of properties and assets.
Just what does he mean by properties and assets? Does he mean, for instance, the lands of the subsidiary companies, meals in the hotels, the Chateau Laurier, 'and so forth?

I should have
thought it would be quite clear. What is referred to is the sale of property which is entrusted to the board for management, not for sale; in other words, capital assets ought not to be disposed of without the consent of parliament or the government.

There is a list

Properties that are required for railway purposes?

I do not know.
