I am not talking of the Canadian Pacific, but of the sale of our own property.

My hon. friend has been
talking very liberally of the Canadian Pacific lately. No, Mr. Speaker, if we are to get the Canadian National Railways out of politics,
I am 'afraid my hon. friend's amendment is not heading in the right direction. He is heading them into politics, rather than out of it. As I said before, I do not know what the government's intention is in regard to the amendment, but for myself I would not feel at all grieved if they refused to accept the amendment as it is proposed.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to discuss this question from one or two angles. In the report presented by the Minister of Railways there is a reference, at page 2624 of Hansard, to wages and labour. Various demands I know have been made by the employees for an increase in wages. However, there have been no strikes, and a general good feeling prevails among all classes on the Canadian National Railways. This is as it should be. Since Sir Henry Thornton has assumed the management of this system a great improvement has been achieved in this respect. While 58.4 per cent of all operating expenses seems high, entailing the sum of 8136,463,470, still I want to urge upon this House that the matter of wages as well as other matters of management and operation Should be left to the good judgment of the president and his board.
The hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Mc-Crea), speaking in the budget debate a few days ago, said that an honest day's work was not given for an honest day's pay, and he quoted some figures which would lead the people of this country to believe that we were in the grip of a railway workers' union. I have made some inquiries regarding the statements of the hon. member, and I find the conditions he cites as to overtime are almost an impossibility. I have had sent me by the Telegraphers' Union, in the city of Saskatoon, a copy of a letter challenging the hon. member to prove his statements. I will read a part of it, sufficient to show that the hon. member has been misinformed by someone. It says:	.
Eighty two representatives of the eight thousand telegraphers employed on Canadian railroads, who are now in convention at Cleveland, instruct that vigorous
protest be filed in parliament against the serious misrepresentation made by Mr. McCrea, member for Sherbrooke, Quebec, on May thirteenth, respecting station agents' salaries. Telegraphers have had their compensation reduced by two and a half million dollars a year since January, nineteen twenty-one, the period he quotes. No agent receives free dwelling. All pay rentals through deductions on payroll. We Challenge the member to name the stations and details of earnings as stated in his speech, knowing his information to be incorrect. There are ninety six working hours in two weeks' pay period. No man could work one hundred and sixty one hours overtime in two weeks without serious results to himself and grave danger to the safe handling of trains. If done, the responsibility rests solely upon the company requiring the service for overworking the employee and piling up cost because the employment of a second man would have been much cheaper.
I know wages are high, but while our manufacturing and distributing combines are protected and hedged about by tariffs, dumping acts and so on, Which places all these concerns beyond the pale of competition, the cost of living must necessarily be high, and we cannot blame any collective body of labour men for at least organizing to maintain a decent standard of living. If we want to lower the wages on our railroads, and bring down as well the cost of freight, we have to lower the cost of living, and it is in the power of the legislators of this country to do that. But that is another tale.
What I want to protest against are these pinpricks by politicians in this House who have no other end in view than to worry Sir Henry Thornton and his board into giving up the job of managing the finest system of railways in the whole world. They would like to see this great Canadian National system again fall into private hands, but I think the people of Canada, and I think I am right in saying the people of all Canada, are proud of their own railway. I do know that in the West we are proud of it, and since Sir Henry Thornton has assumed the presidency there has been a noticeable improvement in the attitude of every employee, and1 a service is given that cannot be equalled in this continent by any railway under like conditions.
This pinpricking campaign that is now carried on by those who, in. past times were short sighted enough to keep up a howl, under the guise of patriotism, that all the trade of this country should go east and west, must stop. That policy was a mistake. To it is due the fact that we have a superfluity of transcontinental lines. Rather than take the backward step of reverting to private ownership this country must now meet the losses occasioned by those very same advocates of private ownership. What the people have



Minister's Statement
they will hold no matter what the cost may be. It will only be a matter of a few short years, I think, when the annual dteficit will be a thing of the past. Rather than go back to private ownership of railways we should be looking forward to the time when transportation will be a great public utility and will be publicly owned. Then, and then only will it be possible to eliminate the great duplication of service which now exists, and render lighter the cost of transportation which bears so heavily upon the people at the present time.
What we want in. this House is a few patriots who can look at things from a national standpoint, from the standpoint of the people, rather than allow themselves to be actuated by narrow motives of selfish interest. It is not very fair to the Canadian National Railways that matters are being discussed here over and over again from the standpoint of the Cauadian Pacific Railway. Let us see whether we owe anything to . that company. I he Canadian Pacific has already been given in land grants and subsidies by the Dominion, provincial and municipal governments enough to capitalize their entire stretch of steel at something like $40,000 per mile. I can give some particulars of the aid which the Canadian Pacific has received. It has received in land grants from the Dominion and provinces 28,816,000 acres. In subsidies it has received $41,544,272; and in lines handed over completed by the Dominion government $37,785,000, or altogether, in addition to land, nearly $80,000,000. Now the land given to the Canadian Pacific amounts to 28,816,000 acres and if we price this land at the very moderate sum of $21.50 we shall have a total of nearly $620,000,000. That added to the subsidized lines completed, and other forms of assistance, amounts to nearly $700,000,000 which up to the year 1920 would have capitalized the whole stretch of steel of the Canadian Pacific at $40,000 per mile.
I think it is 'time we altered our policy and built our public utilities for the public instead of for private concerns who, in times past, have exploited rather than served those who made the concessions. The mistakes of the past are every day becoming more apparent. During the last season of grain transportation -1923-24-very little grain came east after the close of navigation on the lakes. Now, the two natural outlets for western Canada are certainly Vancouver and Hudson bay. But the selfish policy in the past of concentrating our financial and industrial concerns in Montreal and other eastern cities has brought on this country a railway problem of the first magnitude.

I say the Hudson Bay railway must be finished, and it will be completed. In western Canada the farmers have got to find the easiest access possible to the markets of the world, and this country cannot hope any longer to saddle the deficit caused by a superfluity of railway transcontinental lines upon the prairie farmers. In the future they cannot be expected to bear the mistakes that have been made. Indeed, I should like to serve notice right now that the prairie provinces are not to be expected any longer to pay freight charges over an extra mileage equal to the distance between Port Arthur and Montreal, on their products destined for the markets of Europe, even for the purpose -imperative in the eyes of some eastern interests-of making the transcontinental line; pay dividends. There is a problem here which w7e have got to solve. We must face it now and parliament would be better employed in the solution of this question than in jabbing Sir Henry Thornton below the belt. The desire of the people is for co-operation with the management of the Canadian National Railways and they intend to keep that system as their own.

I have been an interested listener to the debate which has so far taken place because the theme is a very important one. In fact,
I doubt if there is any subject before parliament of greater importance than the one we are now discussing. Its importance is due to the tremendous amount of money which parliament is handling as trustees of the people, an amount, I believe, which runs into hundreds of millions. As a previous speaker has stated we are directors of the greatest railway business in the world. I have an idea that at least the important countries of the world have their eyes directed towards Canada, to see whether we are going to make good or not. We are operating under our Canadian National Railway system almost 22,000 miles of railway. We are employing in the neighbourhood of 100,000 men. We have a telegraph mileage in the neighbourhood of 100,000 miles of wire, and we have control of an express company reaching almost all -over Canada, and to some parts of Europe. Not only that but we have a merchant marine totalling 60 vessels in all. We have a chain of hotels in strategical places throughout the Dominion of Canada. All these activities come under the management of our Canadian National Railways.
We might think of this management as being focused in the one individual, the president. His name has been mentioned some-

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
times in a commendable way, and sometimes in a critical way. But Sir Henry Thornton is a big man. I think those of us who have seen him are agreed that he is big physically, and it is my opinion, Mr. Speaker, that his mentality is also very large. It is true he has nine other directors to assist him in the management of this system; but their location stretches from New Glasgow, Nova Scotia, on the east to Prince Rupert, British Columbia, on the west, and it is very hard for them to get together in one place to advise the president. Bj'' the way, I notice in looking over the list of directors that there does not happen to be one with a residence in the province of Saskatchewan. I rather think that is a mistake. Iam convinced in my own mind that if we had a real snappy farmer from Saskatchewan on that board of directors there would not have been the necessity for asking so many questions about the Scribe hotel. I am quite sure a real practical farmer would have weighed the matter so carefully and advised so wisely that the deal would have been delayed. But, we have this board of directors, and their duties are to operate the trains and to see that freight is carried expeditiously, that passengers are moved about, express handled, and so on. They are naturally obliged to retain the good will of the men who are working, so that they may decrease expenditure, increase revenues and continue to secure more business for the system.
We might ask ourselves, why are we in this big railway business? I think the answer has been given very well by the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean). He stated in effect that we were in it because we could not help it. The system of private ownership broke down. . If a mortgage company had a mortgage on a parcel of land, and the farmer decamped and did not make good naturally the mortgage company would take over the land. That is just what happened with our railway systems. The private owners fell down. They were not able to make good, and of course the systems came to the government for operation. When the systems were taken over under the presidency of D. B. Hanna there wras considerable improvement in the service. I happen to live in a town that is touched by a part of the Canadian National system, and the improvement in the service under the presidency of D. B. Hanna was very noticeable, but there was still room for improvement. There were too many officials and sub-officials flying around, who were not earning their salaries. There was too much extravagance. There was also room for improvement in a good many lines. Under the present president conditions have
improved considerably. We had the good fortune in the winter of 1923, shortly after Sir Henry Thornton assumed office, to have him visit the town where I live in western Canada. The impression made by him in that town was a very favourable one. He impressed us, of course, as being just as human as most people. He impressed us as being a man who was liable to make a mistake; in fact there are not very many men who try to do things who are not liable to make a mistake. But in spite of those impressions he also impressed us as being the type of man who was likely to make good.
I need not deal with the financial condition; that has been discussed by the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill). He has given figures to show our expenditures are gradually decreasing, and that our revenues at the same time are increasing, and let us bear in mind that the present management has only been holding office for about one and a half years. Let us remember that the president has asked us to give him three year's' time- I believe three years was the time limit he put-and has said that at the end of that time the road would be pulled out of the hole and that instead of being a debt producing asset it would be a revenue producing concern. This condition will be brought about largely through the calibre of the man who is president. The hon. member for Pontiac wished to give some of the credit to the government, but it is only a shadow of the credit that goes to the government. I believe the real credit goes to the president of the National Railways for the success that has been made of the system during the past year and a half.
What should be the attitude, Mr. Speaker, of this parliament towards the system that has been forced upon us? I was rather disconcerted, to say the least of it, to find, during the first session of parliament that I attended, that so many members rose in their places and spoke disparagingly of the Canadian National system. I could not understand why they should do so. It was our own system and was on our hands. It was our own money that was invested in it. It was up to us to make good or to lose and I could not understand during that session why so many hon. members spoke as they did. Last session I noticed quite a difference in the tone of hon. members in this House. There seemed to be a different feeling towards our Canadian National system, and I believe that that good feeling in favour of our system is growing, not only in this House but throughout the country. There are
C.N.R.-Minister's Statement

eight and three-quarter million people throughout Canada who are anxious that this system should succeed, and we, the representatives of the people of Canada, should all be anxious to see it succeed. It is right enough that constructive criticism should be offered, but such criticism as the suggestion that we should sell our entire system for a dollar or even- less is not going to help promote the welfare of the system now in our possession.
Referring to the amendment proposed by the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton), it was intimated, I believe, by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) that he felt the amendment was going in the right direction. Well, Mr. Speaker, to my mind it seems to be a sort of Jacob-Esau amendment. It feels something like Esau to the blind Isaac, but the
10 p.m. voice, the tenor, or, the intent of it, is more like Jacob. The amendment calls for a select standing committee to consider the estimates. There may not be anything wrong with that, but it asks further that the committee consider all questions involving new capital commitments. Let us consider what that means. All questions involving new capital commitments would have to come before the select standing committee for their approval. That would mean, I take it, that such a simple matter as the purchase of a railway coach would have to be referred to the committee; such a matter as the purchase of steel for our much needed extensions would have to come before the committee; in other words, any and every matter appertaining to new capital commitments would first have to be passed upon by the committee. That would seem absurd. This House is not always in session; there are some six or seven months of the year when we are not here and the committee would not be available. If, therefore, the management desired to place an order for some equipment that was found to be necessary in September or October they would be tied up until parliament convened and this committee got together.
Further the amendment asks that the committee consider the disposition of properties and assets and that too would be a dangerous duty devolving upon a parliamentary committee. As regards the suggestion with reference to annual reports, there would not seem to be much to find fault with in that connection. But it seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that this committee would have altogether too much power. If I understand the intent of the amendment, the committee would have

power to send for papers and records and to consider all business deals, calling for witnesses as it might deem proper. It seems to me that this committee would so circumscribe the president of the Canadian National Railways that he would be left inactive and unable to carry on his business; in fact, he would be just a figure head. And what would the result be? From my knowledge of the president of our railways, I think he would not be very long in the president's chair before he would be looking for a position in which he would have room to move and to act.
The mover of the amendment may not intend such drastic results but it would appear to me that what I have suggested would be the outcome. I fail to see the need of having a committee of investigation. I can remember that for several days our order paper was almost filled with questions and answers in regard to Hotel Scribe and a certain Aronovici, besides questions relating to the Canadian National Railway business generally. So far as I can see there is a ready source and there are ample means of obtaining information, and to appoint a special committee to sit as a sort of trial judge over the president and the directors of the Canadian National Railways would be taking a step in the wrong direction. For my part I do not feel that I can support the amendment.

The excellent showing made by the Canadian National Railways during the last few years is a matter for mutual congratulation, and it is to be hoped that Sir Henry Thornton's prediction of an operating surplus of $30,000,000 for the year 1924 will be fulfilled. There are still, however, many difficulties to be overcome before the people of Canada can view the whole railway situation with equanimity and complacency. The railways have also made a creditable showing during the first two months of 1924. I have here a statement issued by the Bureau of Statistics for January, 1924, which reads:
Canadian National Railways (Canadian lines) turned an operating deficit of $963,137 for January 1923, into a net operating revenue of $16,989 which was a betterment of $980,126.
I have also a similar statement in regard to February 1924 from which I quote the following:
Whereas in February 1923 the lines had an operating deficit of $2,986,197 this year the deficit was only $768,681 and the operating ratio nvas reduced from 122.27 per cent to 105.22 per cent. Freight train loading was heavier by 69.6 net tons and 2.3 care.
The entire system including the lines in the United States showed an increase in revenues of $1,728,191, a decrease in operating expenses of $774,694 and a reduction in the operating deficit of $2,502,885.

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
It may be said that January and February are months during which the railways usually anticipate losses owing to severe weather and a limited amount of traffic. I was interested in the suggestion which the minister made in presenting his report, that a small quorum of directors be appointed, presumably from Montreal or the adjacent country, who might be called together upon short notice by the president. This might be necessary; but I would point out that there are certain dangers in such a policy. I know of nothing that would lessen the confidence of the people of Canada, at least of the larger part of the country, in the Canadian National Railways, than to have more centralized control in the city of Montreal. I believe Sir Henry Thornton has caught the popular imagination of the Canadian people, and I think he deserves their esteem; I would therefore rather increase his powers than hamper him by the addition of further directors to his board. I would suggest to the minister, however, that if it be necessary to appoint more directors, the agricultural industry should not be overlooked in the selection of these officers. In going over the figures for 1923 I note that grain was the largest single commodity handled by the railways last year; it furnished the largest tonnage of any single item handled. Further, it was carried the longest distance of any commodity handled by the railway. It seems to me, therefore, that if further additions are to be made to the directorate the industry of agriculture ought to be represented on the board.
The question of capitalization has been brought up so often in the House that I hesitate to introduce it again. However, it is a very important question and I was glad to hear the minister announce that it was being considered by the directors. Against Canadian National gross earnings of $254,926,000 in 1923 we had interest or fixed charges amounting to $65,199,000; while the Canadian Pacific Railway with a revenue of $195,837,000 has fixed charges of only $13,470,000. Taking our roads separately for 1923, that is, as they were classified in the statement for 1922, we find that the Canadian Northern had gross earnings of only $1.85 for every dollar of fixed charges; the Grand Trunk Pacific $2.19; the Canadian Government Railways, $1.79 and the Grand Trunk Railway $6.95; while- the Canadian Pacific Railway had $13.98 for every dollar of fixed charges and in 1923 $14.60. In the case of Canadian Government Railways, the investment has been charged up to public debt; and in dealing with these figures I have not taken into account interest or deficit; there has been no pyramiding of interest or
deficit as in the case of the Canadian Northern.
I wish to quote an editorial from the Manitoba Free Press dealing with this subject of capitalization :
The time has now come to consider seriously the proposition, which has been frequently advanced during the past two or three years to cut down the capitalization of the system to a point where it will represent the actual value of the road.
It will not be denied that the capitalization of the Canadian National Railway is far in excess of the physical value of the road. In this huge mountain of debt are embedded all the railway blunders of Canada since the first railway was built.
Of the operators of the Canadian National Railway miracles should not be demanded. They cannot be expected to make surpluses sufficient to pay interest charges upon the present combined capitalization of the system. Faced w-ith the certainty that every year there will be a huge deficit, the directors of the system will inevitably get into the frame of mind which finds expression in the phrase: "What's the use?" If there s bound to be a deficit anyway, why worry whether it is ten or twenty million dollars?
But given a just valuation of the road, the directors can be told that they must meet the fixed charges or make way for others who can. They will have a target to aim at and they will be expected to hit it. This w'ill be much more exhilarating and inspiring than shooting arrows into a bog.
Many hon. members have from time to time put forward claims on behalf of the people of the Maritime provinces for special rate consideration, on the ground that the Intercolonial railway was not built as a purely commercial concern but for military and political purposes. And we must admit the justice of that claim. But, Sir, to a certain extent western Canada is entitled to the same consideration. Our natural channels of trade run north and south, and had there been no interference with that trade by way of tariffs we would have been amply supplied with railways from the United States without a dollar of subsidy from the Dominion treasury, and there would have been no railway problem to-day. But the Dominion parliament decreed otherwise; it decreed that trade should be forced east and west, and railways were built for this purpose, and not primarily with the object of earning dividends. The moment you subsidized a railway you admitted this principle. I submit that as conditions are to-day, and as our railways have been built up, trade between the Maritime provinces and central Canada, trade between central Canada and the prairie provinces, trade between the prairie provinces and British Columbia, is entitled to a reasonable rate, a rate at which business can be carried on, a rate that will permit of an exchange of the basic commodities of these various sections of the country, and that the deficit, if any, must in the last analysis be absorbed by the Dominion treasury.

I say that the Canadian National Railway, in the service it is giving to-day, both freight and passenger, takes second place to no railway on the continent. We are proud of it, and we appreciate what Sir Henry Thornton has done in giving us this service. In my own constituency, and I say this without fear of successful contradiction, in the territory served by the Canadian Pacific there are considerably more complaints of the freight and passenger service than there are in the districts served by the
[Mr. Campbell.!
Canadian National Railways. But when we analyze these figures, it seems to me we are getting a little too much service. If we come down locally to the territory between Montreal and Ottawa, have we not more trains than are required to give the necessary service? Is not the same true of our transcontinental trains? Between here and Toronto it seems to me there are more trains provided than are required to maintain that service. When I was coming to Ottawa recently on the Canadian National train, on leaving Winnipeg I went through the coaches and checked up the passengers in order to arrive at some idea as to the service, and I found only three persons in the first-class coach, leaving Winnipeg, only eight in the colonist car, and only about one-third of the sleeping accommodation taken up. I know that people will complain, and complain bitterly, of any curtailment of the passenger service, but if these figures are placed fairly and squarely before the people of Canada, if they are shown that their grain, their cattle, groceries, lumber, food, the necessaries of life, and the products of their basic industries, are made to pay this $8,500,000 operating loss on passenger service, it seems to me they will get loyally behind the administration of the railways in a reasonable curtailment of service. I would strongly impress upon the minister the necessity of going into this with Sir Henry Thornton and seeing if some arrangement cannot be arrived at, possibly in conjunction with the Canadian Pacific, to curtail some of this service and save the people a great deal of money.
In considering the whole railway situation, it appears to me that we are largely straining at a gnat and swallowing a camel. This House was engaged for over a month in an academic discussion of the tariff. The tariff is very important; we are all interested in it, bu't it is not nearly so important to the people of Canada as transportation. We are vitally interested in the tariff in western Canada; but put the two issues squarely before us and ask us which is the more important, and without a moment's hesitation we will answer transportation, and yet we consider here that a few hours' discussion is all that is necessary for the consideration of this all-important question. It may be only the hand of fate, but it seems to me that we spend a great deal of our time trying to find how many things we can disagree on. We centralize on the tariff, the most contentious issue that comes before the House, and when a great question like transportation is up we pass it by with hardly a moment's notice. I hope in the days to come we will take the matter a little more seriously than we are taking it at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, at this late hour I do not intend to take up the time of the House very long. I just want to mate a few remarks in connection with some suggestions that have been made by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) when this debate on the Canadian National Railways was taken up in this House in the first place. He seemed to think the railway was not doing its duty when it did not spend another $5,000,000 for repairs to rolling stock. To me one of the indisputable proofs of the great improvement that has taken place in our railway system, is that it had not to spend this $5,000,000. I can remember in 1921 going along the Grand Trunk Pacific from Lucerne to Fort Fraser. At that time it was not safe to walk along the aisles of the cars unless you were accustomed to railway travelling. I remember asking the divisional superintendent what effect such a condition of the roadbed had on the rolling stock, and I remember his answer that it was costing the Canadian National Railways millions of dollars each year for repairs to their rolling stock, in not having the roadbed in proper shape. I passed along the same roadbed, over the same railway, about a month before I came to Ottawa, and the roadbed was in entirely different shape. You could walk through the train any place you wanted in comfort. The result of that improvement of the roadbed is that the Canadian National Railways do not have to spend this extra money on repairing their cars. They have put the roadbed in such shape that there is not the tear and wear on the rolling stock that there was when the roadbed was not in shape.
In connection with the amendment how many boards are the Canadian National Railways going to have? First, they will have their president and his board, then they will have to come to a board of this House, then go to the Senate, then if this amendment goes through, come back from the Senate to another board of this House. Where will all that land the Canadian National Railways? In my opinion it will land us, in the first place, without a president and I think we have at the present time a president that Canada has just reason to be proud of, and one whom I hope to see at the head of the railways for many years to come and I think it is up to this House to see that he gets a free hand.
There has been a good deal said in this House about the Hudson Bay railway. Now I do not think it is right that that should ever be loaded on to our Canadian National Railways. If this government has made mistakes, and I think both the old governments have committed themselves to this railway, and it is the dlesire of the government to complete that road, it is up to the government to complete it and then hand it over to the Canadian National Railways and give them a bonus to operate it. But do not let us load on to the man who is trying to make our roads a success, another burden in a railroad of that kind.
I would like to take up some of the time of the House on the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, but as the hour is getting late I do not know that I will. I am pleased to note that the government has disposed of four of these boats under 5,000 tons. I would like to see them dispose of more of them. They have some 28 still on their hands, under 5,000 tons. It would occur to me that those boats could be made use of if new hulls were built for them, and the present machinery put in, and put on the lakes to carry grain. In this way the government would be in a position to compete with the grain carriers on the lakes, and these boats would not cost more than half what a new boat would cost. I think the government would be well advised and fully justified in experimenting with at least five or six of these boats, having new hulls built for them converting them into lake carriers of the latest type and using the machinery they now have in the smaller boats. I see no reason why they could not be made a success, and in that way the government could determine what it would cost to carry grain.
Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM (Minister of Railways and Canals): Mr. Speaker, I was informed the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) wished to speak. I should like him to have the opportunity of doing so but as he does not seem desirous of availing himself of it I shall say a few words and they shall be very brief.
In the first place I point out that this is the first time in the history of the Canadian parliament, as far as I know, that it is proposed1 to refer estimates to a committee. The House is not being asked in this amendment >o do something recommended in a motion proposed by the leader of the opposition when he was at the head of the government, or by the present Prime Minister when he was leader of the opposition. They did not ask for any of the things which are asked for in the present amendment. A reference to their speeches will show that what they proposed has no bearing on what is now suggested here. Let me read the amendment itself:

Does the minister mean
every transaction of the National Railway board?

I am speaking generally.
Very many transactions would not be in the Auditor General's report.

None of the National
Railway board's transactions are in the Auditor General's report.

You will find the transactions of the Canadian Government railways are, and everything in connection with them, I imagine, can be examined if it is so desired. I would raise no objection to that, as that is the usual method of investigation. In this case, however, my hon. friend from West York is asking for a special enactment to provide that the estimates should be sent to a committee; not only that, but that the committee shall have power to call witnesses and examine them under oath. Now, I submit, Mr. Speaker, that if we are going to make a success of the Canadian National Railways it must be by co-operation and not by the establishment of new machinery for the purposes of inquisition, whether inquisition be necessary or not.
What position would it put the management of the Canadian National in, if throughout the year they are liable to be haled before this body of inquisition, whether there is any charge or not, and the railway managers placed on a plane inferior to other managers- not only that, but inferior to members of the House of Commons, because members of the House of Commons can say all these things in committee or in the House, without having to take the oath as to their accuracy, but the board of railway management has to submit to be sworn every year this committee sees fit to investigate what it is doing. I think it is not the right attitude to take if we want to make the system a success. I am in favour of co-operation between parliament and the Canadian National Railway board, and for that reason I am prepared to accept a proposition for a committee along certain lines. I have a precedent for this proposition, a precedent referred to last year by the leader of the opposition himself, and that is a resolution moved by the present Chief Justice of the Exchequer Court, who was a colleague of my right hon. friend for quite a time, a gentleman who knows the inside workings of the Unionist party, and knows the inside workings of that government. He was a member of the Liberal party, and knows the inside workings of that party. He is now in the 173
Exchequer Court, and with this combination of information, his opinion ought to be pretty good. In 1921 he moved the following resolution in this House:
That all words after "that" be struck out and the following inserted in lieu thereof:
Rule 10 of the House of Commons relating to the appointment of the select standing committees of the House, be amended for the present session by adding to the select standing committees of the House for the present session a select standing committee on Railways and Shipping, owned, operated or controlled by the government, and that the special committee appointed to prepare and report the list of members to constitute the standing committees for the present session, be instructed to prepare and report the list of members to compose the select standing committee on Railways and Shipping owned, operated or controlled by the government for the present session.
Mr. Maclean was very careful to make it for the present session, knowing it was an experiment, and he wanted to see how it would work out. That was wisdom. The amendment of my hon. friend makes it a standing committee for the future, and I would not be prepared to do that with any committee, because this is an experiment, and the members of the House of Commons may not care for this experiment once they work it out. What did Mr. Maclean have in his mind? I will read one paragraph from his speech, as I think it conveys what I have in my mind perfectly. He says:
What I seek to do is to afford the opportunity for the management meeting a committee of the parliament oi Canada who represent the people so that, sitting together, they might discuss all the important matters relating to the railway administration,, and I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that only through a parliamentary committee can this be done.
Some of the matters referred to have to be discussed at greater length a little later on, and without making any further remarks I am merely suggesting the resolution to which I think the House might well adhere, and which the government is prepared to accept. It has this feature which was outlined by Mr. Maclean; it brings the management and the committee of the House together, to sit down as man to man and discuss these problems. There would be no question whatever, and no difficulty, in getting all the information that it was possible to have in detail. I admit the accuracy of the suggestion made by my hon. friend from Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael) that it does sometimes seem a little peculiar that a deputy gives the minister the details,, and the minister gives them to the House. Quite often it happens that the minister does not give the same details to the House that the deputy gives him, because his hearing may be bad. I admit there is something incongruous about that. In this trial committee which I have suggested, the deputies could


Minister's Statement
appear with tl?e management of the railway, the deputy acting as a go-between between the government and the board of management. In that way I believe every detail could be secured by this coijnnittee, and would be open to the public as well; so that when we came into the House to discuss the details of estimates, there would be no question about the minister being wrong in his information because the members of this House would have had that information direct from the officials themselves. I would suggest to my hon. friend from West York as a fair compromise in the trying out of this new departure of handing estimates to a committee, which is only an experiment, the proposed resolution which I will read to the House. Of course I would not commit this government or any other government to continue this committee, because it is a real departure in principle from anything we have ever had in this this House. Instead of the resolution moved by my hon. friend, I would copy the resolution proposed by Mr. Maclean partially, but not at such great length. My suggested resolution would read:
That rule 10 of the House of Commons relating to the appointment of the select standing committees of the House be amended for the present session by adding to the select standing committees of the House for the present session a select standing committee on Railways and Shipping, owned, operated or controlled by the government, to which will be referred the estimates of the Canadian National Railway and th<* Canadian Merchant Marine for the present session for consideration and for report to the House, provided however, that nothing in this resolution shall be construed to curtail in any way the full right of discussion in committee of Supply.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: The time which I have had to consider this suggested amendment of the Minister of Railways is very brief. It now amounts to about two seconds and a half. However, the amendment really is not before us except as indicative of the attitude of the minister. His suggestion appears to be that we should submit all the estimates of the Department of Railways and Canals-*
No, no.

Then I have got it
wrongly.
Canadian National Railways and the merchant marine.

There is not much else
except the canals. He desires to submit to this committee the estimates of the Canadian National Railways and the merchant marine

for this session, and provide that the submission to that committee should not affect in any way the right of discussion in committee of the Whole. I think now that I grasp the full meaning of what the minister suggested. I will refer to it as I proceed a little further with the discussion. In commenting on the time at which I spoke, which the minister did not seem to like, I really am surprised that he took exception-
Oh no, I did not care.

I do not care to pursue
a debate until we have some little intimation of where the government Stands. We have had several speeches from hon. members to my left, and one from the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill); but the House was left in entire ignorance of any idea that might be in the minds of the government, much less as to the course ft intended to pursue in respect to a definite motion and a proposal before parliament. Further the Minister of Railways had spoken in debate prior to the speech I made myself. I wondered why he should object to my speaking again. I am not going to make much mention of some rather uncalled-for, wholly unit p.m. founded suggestions or insinua tions, some of which came from the hon. member for Pontiac-and if 1 needed any other reason for ignoring them I consider that sufficient-others of which came from hon. gentlemen to my left, to the effect that if you criticise anything connected with the management of the road you are failing in that idolatry with which the whole nation should look up to the mighty personage at its head; you are laying hands on the Ark of the Covenant; you are stepping on holy ground; nnd you are liable to incur the eternal penalty. To suggest that anything could be wrong or that anything indeed could fall short of perfection in the operation of this system is to commit the unpardonable sin and to be forever debarred from political reward.
I am not one of those who look forward to the Canadian National Railways ever going into private hands. Long before hon. gentlemen opposite became enthusiastic for the National Railways I stood1 in this House and on many a platform in Canada and declared that now that we had them they were to be our property, and that they would be the possession of our people after hon. gentlemen were many years in their political and, I feared, in their physical graves. This is still true; and whether Sir Henry Thornton stays or leaves the roads will still remain the pro-

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
perty of the Canadian people. Why, therefore, these suggestions should be made, that anything at all in the way of criticism or even in the way of proposals for the betterment of the system or of the scheme of management, or of review, is dictated by the foes of the road or, still worse, dictated by friends of a private company, the Canadian Pacific Railway, I know not. I know of no reason for any such imputation; I can only attribute it to mad and mean political animosity.
I became in some degree responsible for a policy" which, however it may have been favoured by others, was certainly not favoured by the Canadian Pacific Railway; and I took the consequences of that position. Many of those prominent in that system came out manfully in opposition to that policy, and to the consequences I submitted. And I would be prepared under similar circumstances to do the same again. I resent therefore, particularly at the hands of those whom also I had to fight in this House, the suggestion that I am affiliated1 or connected with any private company whatever, or that those who speak as I do in this debate have any other object except to safeguard the public welfare.
Yes, the present management of the Canadian National Railways is entitled to fair treatment; so is the present head of the system. I do not know that I have ever observed at the hands of any on this side of the House or of anybody in the Dominion anything but the fairest treatment ever accorded him. I know of no public servant who ever entered the service of Canada who has received as fair, as generous, as flattering treatment as Sir Henry Thornton has been given. Some one suggests that I attacked him before he came; but as usual the one who makes that suggestion takes good care not to quote the attack. No word of attack ever escaped my lips, not even up to now, save where Sir Henry Thornton exceeded the authority given him by his board of directors and the Parliament of Canada, and many months after he had come. Those who think otherwise I now invite, while I am on my feet, to state wherein I attacked him. No; he has had fair treatment at our hands. But I wonder what was the treatment accorded his predecessor by those who now hold everybody associated with the road as sacrosanct, beyond even the suggestion of criticism. Why, day after day in this House no attack was too vicious, no suggestion too mean, no vitriol too heated to pour upon his head. Assertions were made which, if made beyond 173i
the walls of parliament, would have been libellous; and they were made day after day. And even the then leader of the opposition went on the stump and condemned not only the head of the railways but the directors as well as men so associated with other companies which were doing business with the road that they could not honestly discharge the duties of their office. From that party now comes the appeal to hush the lips of all; we must not dare criticise anything. Yea, more than that, we are told that if we see something which we think is wrong, which we know is wrong, we must ignore it; for behold! that is evidence that the man is alive: nobody except a dead man could help making mistakes, says the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham). So that if we find any mistake we must immediately bow down and worship it inasmuch as it is an evidence of activity on the part of the president of the Canadian National Railways. Is that not the argument the minister used?
No.

Those are his words,
then.
No.

At all events, that is
supposed to be the attitude we should assume.
No.

Well, if it is not we
will not assume it; and in not assuming that attitude we are not failing in justice to the system. Now, sir, what is the amendment before the House? The amendment is that there should be some committee with definite powers to review, at such time and under such restraints as will not interfere with the management of the system, the record of the system in the past. The amendment goes further-and I will refer to this second feature before I cover the first fully. It suggests that the future programme of the National Railways be subject to review by that committee, but only to the extent of its capital investments and its proposals to sell the property entrusted to it for mange-ment or in part thereof. I hope hon. gentlemen understand the purpose of the amendment. It is not the intention of the amendment that proposals regarding those things which the directors are there to sell shall first be reviewed by the committee; subject to that review shall be such suggestions only as to the sale of that property which the directors are supposed to manage and not to
C .N Jt-Minister's Statement

sell. These things should first be reviewed by the committee, just as they should now be reviewed by the government and' parliament.
The Minister of Railways takes exception to this second power of the committee. He declares that to refer estimates to a committee of this House is something new. I admit that; estimates have never yet been referred to a special committee of parliament. But the estimates to be referred in this case are not the entire estimates; they differ from the other estimates in one particular, and one very great particular: they refer to the purchase of new property for the people of Canada to be operated by the government railway system, and they refer to the sales of property which we already have decided should be operated and not sold.
Hon. gentlemen will see at a glance that these are estimates of an extraordinary character; in the one case we have estimates and in the other proposals. The estimates which it is here proposed to refer to the committee are estimates of a character that never before, until we acquir'd the National Railways at least, have come before parliament or the government. But it is not altogether a new suggestion that a committee of this House should review estimates. I would not favour submitting to a committee the ordinary estimates which year by year we have reviewed; but I was somewhat surprised that the antagonism of the minister to the review of estimates by a committee should be received with applause by hon. gentlemen to my left. Why, I had to stand in the House three years ago and resist the proposal coming from the very party that sits to my left. The hon. member for Neepawa of that day, Mr. Davis, on frequent occasions pleaded in this House that all the estimates should first be reviewed by a committee, and that until this was done we could never get that retrenchment and economy which we should have. Not only did he so plead, but he was supported by man after man, and while I do not speak positively, I am pretty sure I could name hon. gentlemen opposite who supported his plea. And it was stated repeatedly by the hon. member for Neepawa at that time and by others-I have not reviewed the matter but I now accept the minister's statement that it was wrong-that this system was followed in the British House. According to the minister, it is only adopted in respect of special estimates for the purpose of secrecy. Well, these are special estimates. We do not want them so reviewed for the purpose of secrecy,

but we want them so reviewed because of their special character, and because this will be a committee which will have especially under its custody matters concerning the National Railways and the mercantile marine I do not see any very great objection to testing out the system of special review of estimates by a committee, referring and embracing in its scope, for the time being, any way, simply the limited class of estimates named in the amendment.
But I do not regard that as a vital feature of the amendment. I would be glad to accept some concrete proposal from the government which would cover the other features of the amendment. Cheerfully would I accep* such a proposal. But is the minister's suggestion a concrete proposal? His suggestion is too much like the proposal of the hon. leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke). He wants a committee too. His study of the subject has brought him to that conclusion. But what he wants a committee for he does not know! I asked him specially to tell me, but he did not succeed. I do not believe in appointing committees until we give them definite work to do-definite responsibilities and definite powers. For this reason I argued against the motion of the former hon. member for Halifax, Mr. Maclean, three years ago. You get nowhere by appointing a committee simply on a certain subject, with no special powers and no special duties. This seems to be what is in the mind of the leader of the Progressive party-at least he did not feel like going further until he found out where the government stood. We want a committee, and we want to tell the committee what subjects it should take care of, what its powers should be, and the character of the recommendations it is entrusted to make. What is the value of appointing a committee on the subject of the National Railways and the mercantile marine? "Oh" we are told, "they will co-operate with the directors." Well, I am pretty nearly tired of the word "co-operate" until I know what powers the committee are going to have as distinct from the powers of the directors. I suppose they could co-ordinate too; there would be no objection to that. And perhaps, to borrow the favourite word of the ministry this session in the Speech from the Throne, they could "stabilize" something. We could fill in all these meaningless phrases, but the committee would be a mere nonentity, it would be utterly worthless for the purposes of this House.
Now, does the minister suggest any reason why a committee could not usefully review

C.NJi.-Minister's Statement
the operations of the system that are now closed, subject to the very ample restraints, if not too ample, embodied in th| amendment itself? He suggests no reason at all. In fact he says, "I am prepared to let the Public Accounts committee do that." Well, I am prepared to accept the Public Accounts committee. Let him bring in an amendment to this effect, and I shall be prepared to accept it. The Public Accounts committee cannot do the work now. All the time that we have had the Canadian National Railways we have never been able to review those accounts. I do not care particularly up to what date, but there must be some time when the accounts can be reviewed by the representatives of the people who pay the money. And if the minister is prepared to move in this House that those accounts be dealt with in the same manner as the other accounts of Canada are dealt with by the Public Accounts committee, subject, if he likes, to the restraints embodied in this amendment, which Certainly are complete, then it will be satisfactory to me. And if there is any other restraint that he feels is reasonable and necessary in order to give the management all the scope and all the freedom from embarrassment they need to make the railways a success, then I am prepared to accept that amplification of the restraints embodied in the amendment. Can anything be more reasonable than that? This is all we ask. I shall expect the government to Come forward this session-for evidently they purpose to defeat this amendment-and propose in this House at a very early date, so the work can be undertaken this session, a committee with full powers which the minister suggests should now belong to the committee on public accounts. The minister says there should be no power of summoning witnesses and putting them on oath. I wonder has not the Public Accounts committee that power?
Surely.

It is true that a member must show that he believes that in the public interest there is reason for doing this. Certainly the directorate should be entitled to that protection in any committee. Nobody ever suggested that any parliament should empower a committee to examine men on oath unless someone takes the responsibility of saying that there is reason in the public interest to do it. To all the safeguards against recklessly putting men on oath which now pertain to the Public Accounts commit-* tee, or which would pertain to the minister's case if he moves for a reference to the Public
Accounts committee, there will be no exception taken in this end of the House at all. But is the minister to say that in relation to all other matters affecting the Dominion, all the departments of government in relation to every dollar spent in this or spent in that you can summon the minister himself, you can summon the deputy, you can summon all the officers of the Crown and put them on oath, but in relation to anything affecting the National Railways you cannot put anybody on oath at all, and that whatever you get you must get by co-operation and by sitting down side by side in an aimless and blind committee?
Now, there are some special reasons why we should lose no time in affording this machinery. Never in the history of the late parliament was such machinery resisted. It is true we did not solve all the problems connected with the National Railways, but we solved the most and the biggest of them, and we indicated the line upon which this problem should be solved, but the session of the House at which it was intended to carry on the work of the committee under General Mewburn was not held. We have passed through nearly three sessions, and this government has not made the slightest progress towards providing the machinery for taking care and assuming the duties of review which this parliament allows the public of Canada. We have let years go by and hundreds of millions of dollars have been spent with no system of review at all. Now when we seek this machinery we are told by hon. members that we are pin-pricking the road, that we are doing something awful for which we should be haled before the bar of public opinion, simply because we dare to suggest that the hundreds of millions of the people's money should, under proper safeguard so as not to interfere with the management, be subject to review by the representatives of the people in parliament.
I said there were special reasons why we should lose no time in affording this machinery. I could not help but note that the Minister of Railways in respect to some of those suggestions by my hon. friend to my left, the mover of the amendment, should be so brief as to be totally silent. Brief was he in his main address on the question of the Scribe hotel; stiff briefer is he now. I wonder has this parliament done its duty to the country in relation to that matter? Has this parliament not been under some soporific influence, seemingly wholly unable to reveal to the people the real character of that transaction?
C.N.R.-Minister's Statement

I have had an opportunity this afternoon of reading the correspondence that has been brought down with relation to this matter. Let me say this: The purchase of this hotel in Paris was a breach of law, was a misappropriation of funds, was an exercise of jurisdiction never conferred on any board or any man by the Parliament of Canada. The minister says himself it was a mistake; I compliment him for his frankness in that respect. But three million dollar mistakes are things that the people of this country cannot afford altogether to ignore. Let us examine the circumstances under which this so-called mistake was made.
A gentleman by the name of Aronovici came into the employ of the National Railways apparently on the first of December, 1922. This was about the time the present president of the Canadian Na/tional Railways assumed his duties. He is reported as first of all giving attention to immigration and colonization, some things of that sort-a general securing of business for the road in Europe. For the months of December, January, February, March and the half of April, four and a half months, he was paid for that work $5,625, as shown by a return brought down to this House just a few weeks ago. That is at the rate of $1,100 or $1,200 a month. Some amount!
This money is not to be withdrawn from the Bank of Toronto until the note and interest thereon is paid. It could not be very well used for the interest because it was exactly sufficient to pay for the principal, but the effect of the arrangement is this: The National Railway board took $2,608,000 odd dollars out of the treasury, put it in the Bank of Toronto, asked the Bank of Toronto to send $2,600,000, the same amount, over to France, but to leave this money on deposit. If the money was not paid on six days' notice then they could take the amount on deposit and apply it. Hon. gentlemen are wondering, I know they are, why that method was adopted. Hon. gentlemen are wondering why the company did not send the money over. We deposit the money in the bank, tell the bank to send over the same amount, and bind ourselves to hold that money in the bank and let the bank apply it in payment, if it is not paid after six days' notice. Why in the world go round all these circles? Well, if hon. gentlemen wonder why that was done I think I can tell them. It was because the purchase was illegal from the beginning, and because they wanted to keep it in the shape of pretending to lend the money to Aronovici, and all the while Aronovici was borrowing it here, the bank was lending it to Aronovici. I do not know how otherwise to describe the transaction. The very course pursued shows that the straight course could not legally be pursued. Now, I ask the minister why the money was not taken and sent over? If they had the right to buy that property they had the right to pay for it. They had the money why did they not pay for the property? It is because they wanted to get something which would evade the law and they resorted to subterfuge to get round it. Even trying to do that they did not succeed. I am surprised to find that the Canadian National Railways had no power at all to give that guarantee.

May 81, 1923.
Dear Mr. Graham :
For some months the necessity for a more aggressive campaign in Europe on the part of the Canadian National Railway system has been apparent to me, if we are to get our share of the European business, and likewise develop a constructive immigration policy?
In this connection let me observe that the Canadian National Railway system is not in possession of ocean-carrying passenger vessels and therefore cannot develop an immigration traffic overseas. In this regard it is not in the same position as the Canadian Pacifio Railway.

It is not in the same position as the Canadian Pacific at all. but it can do a great deal in that way providing traffic for the National Railways and directing it thither from other ships. It is true the Canadian National system has not its own vessels, and to that extent it is at a disadvantage; but overseas traffic can be directed to the National roads.
Does the minister mean passenger traffic?
Take immigration traffic for example.

It seems to me that the government could do something in that regard without any special efforts on the part of the National Railways. I do not want to digress from the main subject, but I think there is very valid objection to this government maintaining an expensive immigration service of its own, and our alter ego, the National Railways, maintaining another. And that objection can be pretty well illustrated by just what has developed here. It seems to me that in so far as the question of immigration is made an excuse for this purchase there might well have been some discussion between the government and the president first, because I do not accept the immigration theory at all as any warranty for the purchase of the Scribe hotel. We do not get any immigrants from France; we have not succeeded in securing any for years, the number being virtually negligible. As every one knows, the French government is strongly opposed to 
the encouragement of emigration from that country; and as to diverting emigrants from Europe, I presume something might be done in that direction. There has been abundant evidence that our inactivity abroad was losing us a certain amount of business, and you may recall, for example, the statement made recently on the floor of the House by an hon. member, complaining that the National Railway system was unknown in Europe.
I venture to suggest that the statement was the most expensive utterance ever made on the floor of this House, and I cannot think now to whom I should attribute the responsibility for it.
One of the essential implements in the solicitation of business, as well as for the purpose of advertising the Dominion of Canada as a whole, is proper quarters at strategic European points.
It looks as if we were in for a series of hotels.
We are already properly housed in London but we have no quarters on the continent. I therefore considered it necessary to secure offices of sufficient prominence to meet our requirements in that territory. Early in this month, an opportunity developed to secure a property at' the corner of Rue Scribe and Boulevard des Capucines, close to the place de l'Opera, and in the centre of the banking and transportation district: briefly it may be said that this location is in the very heart of the city.
This had occurred nearly four months, or at least three months before. But that may be merely a mistake of memory.
Immediate action was necessary, as I had known from authentic sources that other interests were considering the property. I think it is nearly $3,000,000. I do not think that the extension of time to 110 years will convert the transaction from a permanent one into a mere matter of temporary financing. There is not the slightest evidence of any temporary financial arrangement to be found on the whole face of the file; not a document, not a suggestion of any kind is there to indicate that the matter is anything but a permanent acquirement of property, save what I read in the latter part of the letter, a very significant feature:
The deal was immediately consummated, and simultaneously negotiations were entered into with a responsible syndicate not connected with the Canadian National Railway system, for the purpose of taking over the property, and with a view to our becoming tenants. These arrangements have now been completed and the syndicate has agreed to take over the property, subject to certain details.
Outside of the assertion of the minister, there is a definite, conclusive, inescapable statement; and the whole file can be searched from beginning to end for the slightest reference to any attempt to get a syndicate or the slightest testimony of the existence of a syndicate at all. The minister told us last session, just as we are told here, that the deal was complete for another syndicate to take the property over, and that we were to be out of the transaction at the price we paid for the property; all of which turns out wholly incorrect. Would that we were out of it! I do not know, though, that the taking over of the property by a syndicate on terms of our renting the property at a figure that would represent a profit to the syndicate would be getting very well out of the transaction. But if there is any way of getting any one to take it at anything approaching the price we paid for it, yes, at half or a good deal less than half what it cost the country, it will be a lot better than our putting up with the loss year after year. I go on:
There will be reserved for. the Canadian National Railway system such space as will be required for its purposes, and also for such departments of the Canadian government as may wish to avail themselves of this opportunity.
Should the provincial governments also wish to take advantage of the opportunity, they will be treated in the same way as the Canadian National Railway system.
The president of a few months of our
National system started out to get accommodation in Paris for the Dominion government
and for the provincial governments without deigning to consult a member of any of the whole ten governments.
It is the intention to locate, if possible, in the building offices for Canadian institutions, so that the property will be and will become known as a Canadian headquarters in Paris and on the Continent.
The "Palais Canadien."
I regard it as fortunate that the Canadian National Railway System has been able to secure such advantageous quarters at a reasonable rental-
By the way, there is nothing in the whole thing to give the slightest indication what the rental is, or even that any rental is payable.
It would be unwise and undersirable in the interests of the Canadian National Railway System that full details of the transaction should be known-
This sentence I enthusiastically concur in.
-until all arrangements have been completed, but I may say for your information that Major Bell, the deputy minister of Railways and Canals and Mr. Gerard Ruel, vice-president in charge of the legal department, have full knowledge of the entire transaction and are prepared to join with me in a complete endorsement.
Well, I find no endorsement on the file. For that I congratulate the two gentlemen referred, to. If there should be one I would say, all the worse for them.
Now we come to the fall, October arrives with nothing on the intervening file at all, not a letter, not a telegram. We are asked to believe that not one single communication passed between the notification to the government in May and the following October. Does anybody imagine that to be correct? Is not this parliament being denied information which we ordered to be revealed? And is there any reason for denying us this information? Is it going to help the Canadian Pacific to the injury of the National Railways that the truth about this should be known? This has not the slightest thing to do with the operation of the system; this is a capital purchase away over in Europe beyond' the scope and beyond the jurisdiction of the directorate altogether, even if rightly done. Certainly there must have been communications between the month of May and the month of October. In the month of October a contract is submitted to the National Railway board for ratification. Apparently Mr. Bell had been in Europe trying to extricate the administration and the directorate from the mess into which they had precipitated themselves. Mr. Bell came back and submitted for approval this contract made between himself-representing the National Railways, but subject to the approval of the board of directors and the Dominion government-and

Mr. Arnold Aronovici. I will read the description of him:
Mr. Arnold Aronovici of Paris, acting in his capacity of temporary proprietor of the building situated at the corner of the Rue Scribe and the Boulevard des Capucmes, Paris, known at the present time as the
Palais Canadien."
That is his description, and I Commend to the delectation of parliament those fine words, "temporary proprietor". Now the terms of this agreement I can give. It is not altogether very clear, but it is an infinite improvement in its clearness, though not in its ultimate effect, on the original agreement upon which it was built and for which apparently it is now a substitute. But, mind you, the terms of the original agreement are what .constituted the weapon which extracted this agreement from the National Railways of Canada, that is, from the treasury of Canada. It is recited that the government had advanced the sum now of 38,232,161.75 francs to Mr. Arnold Aronovici for the purchase of the property. That money was already gone. It included the original purchase price which Arnold Aronovici quoted the National Railways. What his option price was we are never told, we never get a hint of it; in all the answers to our questions it is evaded. That amount included 3,600,000 francs for registration fee to the French government; it included 3,600,000 francs for settling with tenants; in included 300,000 francs for fees and commissions-I wonder where those commissions went unless to Mr. Aronovici-and it included 50,000 francs for sundry expenses. Add those up and there is still a gap between that amount and the 38.000,000 francs which the government paid, and regarding this deficiency we are not favoured with information. Now then, over and above the 38,000,000 francs odd which already the government had advanced-, this agreement made by Mr. Bell-and no doubt he did the very best he could after they got into this position,-called for the payment of 650,000 francs more. Payment to whom? Well, it goes without saying that it was to Mr. Aronovici. He was to get that in order to liberate himself. Let us just contemplate this:
in order to liberate himself from all contracts he may have made to the present time with any parties whatsoever with regard to the "Palais Canadien"-
Arnold Aronovici up to this time held the "Palais Canadian" for the National Railways. If he had made any contracts they were ours. Why in the world would we pay him 650,000 francs to get free of contracts of which we should have had the benefit if

there was any benefit in them? 650,000 francs to liberate himself from his contracts for us. Would that we could have paid the same to liberate us from his! But that is not all:
For architectural work, plans, estimates and expenses -to be justified-in view of transforming the basements, ground floor and first floor of the "Palais Canadien"; 169,000 francs (temporary estimate).
All these things were not included in the original option at all or in the original contract with Arnold- Aronovici. These apparently are just some other methods of getting rid of Aronovici without paying him the 10 per cent commission called -for by the original contract, and I do -not think it will take hon. gentlemen very long to come to that conclusion.
These two sums are to be paid at the latest by the end of December 1923.
But there is a lot more yet:
The sum of 700,000 francs will be held at the disposal of Mr. Arnold Aronovici at the bank before December 31st 1923,-
I should in all fairness explain that this is a translation, from the French, and consequently the language may not sound just as it would in the original. But the meaning is easily got at.
-and he will have to produce a receipt for the said sum from the Societe du Jockey Club, the expense of which receipt will be borne by the C.N.R.
Now, it will be recalled that in the original sum, much less than 38,000,000 francs, there was included 3,600,000 francs for paying off the tenants, of whom the Societe du Jockey Club was c-ne. Now if he can show a receipt from that Jockey Club for some 700,000 francs or under, he is to get that money too, and if he can show a receipt from the Societe Fran^aise La Rente Fonciere-that is, I believe, the company from which he had the option, although I am not certain of that- he is to get up to the balance of the 700,000 francs. Here is provided for this man, in addition to the whole sum, in the first place, of the contract, 650,000 francs to be paid him to liberate him from contracts, 169,000 francs for the plans and 700,000 francs for some other supposed claims that he had in respect of La Rente Fonciere and in respect of La Society du Jockey Club. Now, apparently he is getting more than all this, but what for I do not know. Then, the contract proceeds:
Mr. Aronovici will receive within the period mentioned in article 3, and from the same bank, the amounts due to the Societe Frangaise La Rente Fonciere, for which amounts he will have to produce a receipt from the said company.	'[DOT]
Then there is a lot more, principally to make clear that all further expenses in con-
