nection with this, that and the other thing are to be paid by the Canadian National Railways. In case the Canadian National Railways do not go ahead they are to forfeit 500,000 francs and he is to do the same thing if he does not go ahead. But why he would not go ahead I will ask hon. gentlemen to imagine. Then, the contract is to come into effect when approved by the board of directors and by the Canadian National. There is a provision also that if Madame Aronovici has any claim she must release it too. It is a pity there could not have been something paid to her in order to liberate her from any intricacy in which she might have been involved.
Now this contract was ratified by the Canadian National Railways. The matter then was submitted to the government and on the 17th of December the government passed an order in council congratulating themselves on the splendid bargain that had been made and authorizing the National Railways to go through with it. I do not need to read the order. It recites that they have formed a company among the subsidiaries of the National Railways, a company with power to hold the stock of any other company. So they formed a company in Paris under a French name.
A bad thing, that French name.
Well, I did not say it was. What does the hon. member interject that for?

My right hon. friend
suggested that it was a French name. There was a little inference there.
No, there was no inference. I stated they formed it under a French name, and I did not have the name before me, that was all, I know what the hon. member had in mind.

May I ask the right hon. gentleman a question? Suppose everything he says is true, has he a remedy? Does he suggest a way in which the National Railways can be looked after better than the present government is doing it?

Yes, I think I do, but that is rather a poor escape from the position the hon. member got himself into. Now, I go on. The French company has its stock held by a subsidiary company of the National Railways. The stock of that subsidiary company is of course held by the National Railways. The National Railway stock is held by the government of Canada, so as hon. gentlemen will see, we are the owners of the Scribe hotel. We are the real owners of it by ownership of the stock of the companies
that own it. Now, I ask, where has gone into blank space that syndicate that was to relieve us of this incubus? What has become of it? Did they take a look at the Scribe hotel or take a look at Aronovici? If so, what was the reason of their vanishing into thin air? We have heard nothing of this syndicate this session except that it does not exist. I do not doubt for a minute that the government have scurried about the financial offices of New York trying to get somebody to make some sort of deal to relieve us of this white elephant. I do not doubt it for a minute, because the government assured this House last session that the syndicate deal was complete, just as the government was assured it was complete by Sir Henry Thornton himself. Under this delusion the members of the House rested for many months.

I do not think the government said it was complete, because on several occasions I asked the Minister of Railways and Canals whether he had any information to give the House as to the completion of the deal and he said he had not.
Was not the hon. member's question as to the personnel?
No, I asked him-

I think so. The minister would not give us the personnel. He stated it was a mere temporary financing; that arrangements had been made to take it over, and Sir Henry Thornton had so stated to the minister in writing, in his letter of the 31st of May. I know the minister would not give us names, and I never could understand why. He said it would be bad in the making of arrangements with the tenants in the Scribe hotel, as if it made any difference to the tenants who owned the building or who did not; if they had to get out they would make the best terms they could. I could never see any force in the reason the minister gave, and I do not think the hon. member for George-Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) saw any force in it either.

If the right hon. gentleman will pardon me, I asked the minister in the last days of the session whether he had any information to give the House as to the completion of the deal with the New York syndicate, and he said he did not have any information.

That may have been the way the hon. member put it of course I could not be expected to remember the exact wording. But I put myself in the judgment of hon. members of this House of all
C.N.R.-Minister's Statement

parties if in the original discussion the minister did not give us to understand precisely what Sir Henry Thornton gave him to understand: That the syndicate arrangements were completed but that he could not reveal the names because of the negotiations pending between the syndicate and the tenants of the Scribe hotel.
Now, this House has a right to understand this transaction. Some hon. members may want to pass it over as a mere mistake; that, of course, is their privilege. . Those who take a more serious view of their responsibilities to the people for the money of Canada will certainly, I think, take a loftier attitude toward the subject than that. I ask hon. members to read this correspondence from end to end, all of it that is revealed. Ask yourselves first, is this a real record of the transaction, a complete record, or is it not ? If you feel it is not, ask yourselves, why is^ the intervening correspondence not here? Why is there not something to tell us what took place between those awful gaps? Ask yourselves next, is this whole contract such as to inspire confidence in the management of that great system? That it is an excess of jurisdiction all of us know, and it is more than an excess of jurisdiction. Just imagine the position this parliament is in. For years this parliament and the government of Canada have looked forward to the time when we could . get suitable quarters in London, England. We have never felt we were in a position to do so, even at the price of a million dollars and something over. But without being asked at all, without the slightest consultation, without even the government being apprised of the negotiations, the president of the National Railways calmly plants nearly twice that amount in the Rue des Capucines in Paris.-and that is what is described as a mere mistake.
I want hon. members to reflect on two or three other features of this correspondence.
I wonder did the minister observe that in that letter to him of 31st May, in which the first information was given him of the transaction, so we are asked to believe, Sir Henry Thornton describes its merits and all about it, or is supposed to have done so, and he never tells the minister the cost; he does not even indicate what it was costing at all. Did he consider that of no importance? Let the minister look through the correspondence and he will find that in the whole body of it there is not a single valuation by a solitary soul of the Scribe hotel in Paris, not the slightest word to justify the opinion of any human being that the property was worth 
the money paid-not only no word, but an utter absence of reply from the only gentleman to whom Sir Henry Thornton ever appealed to get a valuation of the property.
LTnder those circumstances I ask hon. members to sit down and think of the responsibilities of this parliament. Are we going to go on in this fashion, or are we going to have some means by which transactions can be reviewed, and reviewed in time to be of some service, that is as respects at least further investments of the Canadian people in capital acquirement? We cannot review, to be of some service, mere matters of operation. That is impossible, but because such is impossible let us not disrobe ourselves of the responsibility that we have such as we can effectively exercise. Let us live up to .our responsibility to the best of our capacity. Now I ask the minister, if he is determined that the House shall vote down this resolution, not to let many days elapse before he does bring down a plan to parliament in line with the recommendations in his address, some line that we can pursue, some path that we can follow by which we can discharge responsibilities that are justly and inescapably our own.

Supposing this whole
Hotel Scribe proposition is wrong: what proposition has my right hon. friend to put before parliament whereby our railways may be run without interference from parliament?

There is one embodied
in the amendment. Under the law as it stands to-day the government of Canada must advance to the railways, their prior assent being secured, moneys for capital investment. The railway company has no authority save what parliament gives it. It could not have any authority save that. It is a parliamentary creation. We have never given .it that authority. Such is the law to-day. My first remedy then is that the government see to it that there is no excessive jurisdiction exercised by the National Railway board, that when it is done, instead of passing a blessing upon it and standing in this House and defending it, as the Minister of Railways did a year ago, he severely reprimand the president of the railways and let him understand that that kind of thing cannot be pursued, that investments of that kind are not of the nature of investments that are required in the ordinary course of operation. They are just as far the antithesis of it as you could conceive. Next, when it is done, that the government do not pass an order in council, as they did in this case, approving of it and declaring what I do not think they believed and what

C.NJt.-Minister's Statement
the minister at this session has admitted that he does not believe that it was in the interests of Canada. That is my first suggestion. Second, that we take the additional precaution in respect of these matters that are new in their responsibility, of having a committee of this kind review them, review them not in any way detracting from the power of the whole committee of parliament, but review them by way of additional precaution. Thirdly, I would recommend that we have a standing committee which under proper restraints, at a sufficiently subsequent time, can take before it all expenditures of the railways, and if it is believed that the investigation of any is in the public interest, investigate them effectively and finally. This, I believe, will be a restraint upon the perpetuation of the system that has already been launched in that railway.

I have no doubt in the world as to the broad-minded view taken by my right hon. friend, but if there is going to be a railway in this country, I would ask him who is going to have the management of that road-a committee of parliament or the management to which parliament has already turned over the roads. If that management does wrong, I presume the Minister of Railways is responsible, but I fail to see the ground that my right hon. friend takes when he says: You may have a railway in this country, you hand over the management to them. If they go wrong, then there is something that is certainly almost libellous that may be cast towards my hon. friend the Minister of Railways. I would ask my hon. friend how were the National Railways conducted for two years previous to the advent of this government to power? You had a board of operators at Montreal. Did you take full responsibility for them? I suppose you should.

I have answered the hon. member. His first question was: Who should manage it? As I have stated repeatedly, and as I wish to emphasize now, the management should be undoubtedly in the unrestrained control of the directorate.
Absolutely.

Now my hon. friend asks, how was it managed before? In accordance with that very principle. No acquisition of new property such as this, or any other property not a mere detail of operation, was ever launched upon by the old directorate without a prior vote of parliament and the authorization of the government.
Suppose a question came up necessitating a quick decision. Would my hon. friend come to parliament or the government for that?

There is no quick procedure ever needed in any matter of acquisition of capital; there never was. Who would suggest that this procedure was needed or should have been done quickly? It is not practically necessary. As a matter of fact, at that time parliament was sitting.

Mr. Speaker, it is certainly with a considerable degree of diffidence that I rise at this late hour to speak on this question of very great importance, and particularly in reply to the right hon. gentleman who for an hour or more has criticised this agreement for the purchase of the Scribe hotel and the arrangements made in connection with the purchase price. I quite appreciate that the right hon. gentleman is quite sincere in his criticism, and that the hon. member for West York is quite sincere in his resolution in which he asks for a committee of inquiry. I am opposed to the hon. gentleman's amendment for a committee of inquiry, and I am likewise opposed to the suggestion of the hon. Minister of Railways. I think that the resolution of the hon. member for West York goes too far. I think that the suggestion of the hon. Minister of Railways does not go far enough, and that it is not in the right direction.
It is suggested that the management of the Canadian National Railways should be kept out of politics. That was the suggestion made by the former government when this railway system was acquired by them, and with that principle every man in this country is in perfect accord. There is no man in this House or in this country who has for one moment the idea that the Canadian National Railway system can be operated successfully if political influences are allowed to intervene or to influence the action of the executive of that organization in the slightest degree. If such were to take place, the road would be a failure from the start. Human nature is much the same whether it is enclosed in the skin of a Tory, a Liberal or a Progressive. I have not much doubt but that when the Liberals were in opposition they perhaps unduly and perhaps improperly criticised the action of the former government and the action of the Canadian National Railway management. I am very much inclined to believe that if a Conservative government were in power now, and if a branch line bill had



C.NJi.-Minister's Statement
been brought down and had passed this House and gone to the Senate, constituted as it is, we would not have seen the opposition in the Senate that we see to-day to the branch line bills that are now before it. I am very strongly of the belief-I do not wish to attribute improper motives to anybody-that had a Conservative government been in power we would not have had a resolution from Senator Bennett-
Order.
-calling for an investigation of the Canadian National Railway system.
Order.
I call the attention of the hon. member to the well known rule that no criticism of the Upper House is permissible in this chamber.
I ask, Mr. Speaker, that you relax your ruling to the extent of enabling the hon. member to explain the position of Liberal senators on the same question.

I am not excusing Liberal senators any more than I am excusing Conservative senators. With the permission of the Speaker and of the House I would say it is suggested in the newspapers that some Liberal senators are like some Conservative senators-they are very much bound up in the interests of the Canadian Pacific Railway. But the Canadian National Railway Company is managed in such a way at the present time that I believe we are bound to have the intervention of politics to a greater or lesser extent. This should not be the case, and before I sit down I intend to propose a new arrangement whereby, I think, politics will be eliminated entirely.
The leader of the opposition devoted his speech very largely, in fact almost entirely, to a criticism of the purchase of the hotel property in Paris. He has had the opportunity-which I have not had although I might have had had I been as diligent as he has been-of examining the papers. It seems to me, however, that the real thing to consider, the real gist of the transaction, is this: Has the property cost the Canadian National Railways what it is worth and no more than it is worth? Whatever may have been done in the way of purchasing the property, whatever may have been said in regard to the formation of a subsidiary company or companies to take over the property and hold it in trust for the government, whatever may be said about the agreement or about the action of Sir Henry Thornton in regard to the initiation of the proceedings or in regard to

the commissions paid to this Roumanian gentleman who had the handling of the affair -whatever I submit may be said with regard to .all these matters it comes down at last in the final analysis to this question:	Have we got value	for our
money? If we have then I submit, Mr. Speaker, that all these criticisms regarding the manner in which the property was purchased fall to the ground. There may have been mistakes made, I do not know. I do not intend to excuse a man even for making a mistake, or a glaring mistake such as is suggested has been made here; but if there have been mistakes made the only man really who can explain to this House and to the country the true inwardness of the transaction is Sir Henry Thornton himself. He is the naan I would like to have before this House. I should like to have him appear before parliament-not only before the members of the House but before the members of the Senate as well-and make a statement. Now here is the plan I would suggest for keeping the Canadian National Railway system out of politics:	It has been said
that the Canadian National Railway Company is a company with one shareholder, the government of Canada. So long as that idea prevails there will be politics mixed up with the management of the company and there cannot be any other result. I say that the shareholders of the Canadian National Railway Company are composed of about eight million people. The shareholders number eight million and those people should be represented here at an annual meeting of the company. It is impossible, however, to have the whole of the people 'attend at an annual meeting. It is not possible to have even all the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company attend at their annual meeting. In actual practice I do not suppose that one-tenth of the Canadian Pacific shareholders attend at an annual meeting. But we do have the representatives of the whole of the people assembled in parliament every year. Now as parliament is in session every year in the month of March-as it must necessarily be in consequence of the financial year expiring at the end of that month-why is it not possible for parliament to temporarily postpone its customary work and for the members of the House and senators to meet in this chamber, or in some other room equally accessible and equally commodious, not as members of parliament, not as members of the Conservative party or as of the Liberal party or of the Progressive party; not with the Prime Min-

C.N.R.-Minister's Statement
ister at the head of one party and the leader of the opposition at the head of another party; but meet here absolutely as shareholders in the Canadian National Railway Company, with the president,

Sir Henry Thornton or whoever he may be-sitting at the head of the table presenting the financial statement for the year, explaining the operations of the system for the past year and perhaps the operations of the company for the succeeding year. Then allow these shareholders, the representatives of the people-members of the Senate and House of Commons-to select the board of directors by ballot each year. I do not think it is best in the interest of the Canadian National Railway Company that the government of Canada should select the directors as they are doing now. Even if part were selected by the government, part by the Conservatives, and part by the Progressives there would still be criticism. I do submit that the directors should be selected in the same way the directors of any other incorporated company are selected, by ballot of the shareholders, the shareholders in this case being the members of the Parliament of Canada. Then we would have a board of directors in whom all parties in Canada would have confidence. We could then have the annual statement of the president of the company laying before us the past actions of the company and perhaps the proposals for the future. If the president had branch lines to build that proposition would be submitted to the members of the Canadian parliament, assembled not as partisans but simply as shareholders in the company. If that scheme were adopted I believe you would have a board of management from which the political element would be eliminated.

Would you expect the
whole number of shareholders, the entire population of nine millions, of Canada to vote on this question?
I do not know how many shareholders there are in the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. I venture to say there are pretty close to a million.

Very well, 140,000, and I do not suppose that three hundred, or two hundred, or perhaps even one hundred attend the annual meeting. Whereas at this meeting of the representatives of the shareholders of the Canadian National Railway Company we would have 235 members of the House of Commons and 100 members, or thereabouts, 171J
of the Senate, representing the people of Canada, holding what you might call statutory proxies for the people whom they represent, and they would sit here as shareholders. You would then have the whole financial affairs of the company placed before this large committee, not a small committee as suggested by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) and not a committee as suggested by the hon. member for West York. It seems to me- and it may not meet the views of anyone but myself-that something of that kind could be worked out whereby, as far as humanly possible, the political element could be eliminated entirely from the operation of the Canadian National Railway Company. I would like to see that done, and I am sure Conservatives as well as Liberals would like to see it done; then under the management of Sir Henry Thornton I would have no fear whatever -of the future success of the Canadian 'National Railway system.
Great credit is due Sir Henry Thornton. He came here at a most critical time in the history of the Canadian National Railway system. He was a new man in Canada, almost entirely unacquainted with the country, its necessities and possibilities. He has acquired a thorough knowledge of the whole country, from the Atlantic to the Pacific. He has brought the standard of the Canadian National Railways up to a pitch equal to that of any system of railways on the American continent. I live in a section of Ontario Which is served very largely by the old Grand Trunk system and the Canadian Northern system. The difference between the operation of the road now and the operation under the old system is so marked that we cannot help appreciating the capability of the management behind the operations which have brought about that great change, and I hope to see some scheme devised by which the political element will be entirely eliminated.
Regarding the question which has been so fully discussed by the leader of the opposition, I can only say that I am not sufficiently conversant with it to go fully into the details as he has done, but my information is that the building and the property which have been purchased are full value for the money which has been paid for them, if not more. I think it is a property which will be of great benefit to the Canadian National Railway system, and when the full particulars of the transaction are known, as in all probability they will be before this session is closed, it will be found that the criticisms of the leader of
